core_operation: Semantic-type detection from a column profile: the pool score of each token is computed only from rotation-invariant scalar statistics of its state and never from its direction.
mechanism: For each token state x_i (32-d), compute scalars: norm, mean, std, skew, kurtosis, fraction of positive coordinates, L1/L2 ratio, cosine to the line's mean state, cosine to the mean of the two least-norm tokens, and the same statistics of x_i minus the line mean. Run a 2-layer MLP (16 hidden units) on these scalars to get 3 role logits per token, with a softmax over tokens per role. Role-k readout is s_k = Σ_i softmax_i(logit_ik)·x_i. Key = W·s_person and value = V·[s_value; s_rel]. The scorer is blind to the direction of x_i, so it cannot memorise the 16 training names. It can only learn how a person-type column is distributed.
why_novel_names: A rule built on invariant statistics cannot depend on which 16 vectors were seen. Any unseen name drawn from the same distribution has the same profile and gets the same role score.
nearest_known: Attention pooling with role-specific projections. The difference is that the scorer input is restricted to a direction-free statistics profile, as in column-type detection (Sherlock/Sato). It is an invariance bottleneck on the selector and is not a typed projection of the state.
prediction: The gap between familiar and novel accuracy shrinks from about 0.41 to under 0.2, and novel person-lost errors drop by about 10 points. Familiar accuracy may drop by about 0.02.
lens: databases: how a key is formed when the key value has never been seen

core_operation: A foreign-key semi-join through the leak: anchor on the value token, take its residual trace of the neighbouring person, and join that trace against all tokens in a learned trace space to retrieve the clean person vector.
mechanism: Step 1: an anchor distribution over tokens, α = softmax(u·x_i), is meant to land on the value token. It is a closed 24-class vocabulary, so the detector generalises. Step 2: the trace is t = P(Σ α_i x_i), where P is a learned 32×32 matrix that maps the anchor's leaked component into person space. Step 3: join scores j_i = cos(t, Q x_i)·γ over all tokens, with the anchor excluded by multiplying by (1 − α_i). Step 4: the person vector is p = Σ softmax(j)_i x_i. Key = W[p; rel readout], value = V·(Σ α_i x_i). Params are about 4k. The answer-only gradient shapes P and Q. Nothing stores a name, because the join is by similarity to a leaked trace.
why_novel_names: The weak identity trace of a name is a linear echo of its token vector. A linear map that aligns the echo to the clean vector works for any vector, seen or not. Retrieval is content-addressed by the echo and never by name identity.
nearest_known: Self-attention layers then pool; induction-head-style two-hop attention. The difference is that the query is the learned residual trace of a detected anchor token, and the lookup excludes the anchor and uses its own trace-space metric.
prediction: Cards whose person identity is a weak echo are replaced by cards holding the clean person vector. Person-lost errors on novel names drop from about 43% to about 28%.
lens: databases: how a key is formed when the key value has never been seen

core_operation: Cardinality-constrained role assignment with a dustbin (UNIQUE / exactly-one constraint) via Sinkhorn: each of the three roles takes exactly one unit of token mass and 7 units go to a filler bin.
mechanism: Build a score matrix S (10 tokens × 4 bins: person, relation, value, dustbin) from learned bin vectors, S = X B^T. Run 5 Sinkhorn iterations with column marginals (1,1,1,7) and row marginals 1, giving an assignment matrix M. Role readouts are s_k = Σ_i M_ik x_i. Key = W[s_person; s_rel] and value = V s_value. Mass conservation means that if a token is strongly claimed by the relation or value bins, which are closed and well learned, it cannot also be the person. The person bin is then forced onto the remaining content token even when that token looks unfamiliar. Params are about 2k.
why_novel_names: The person bin does not need to recognise a name. It receives the token that the recognisable closed-class bins and the dustbin have left over, through the transport constraint. This is exclusion by conservation.
nearest_known: Slot attention and SuperGlue-style matching. The difference is a hard exact-marginal optimal-transport plan with fixed cardinalities, (1,1,1,7), enforced across tokens. Slot attention only normalises softmax over slots and has no cardinality constraint.
prediction: Novel person-lost errors fall by about 12 points and novel accuracy rises by about +0.09. The relation-only and person-only confusions with the decoys decrease.
lens: databases: how a key is formed when the key value has never been seen

core_operation: Frame-of-reference exception encoding with median/MAD: subtract the per-dimension median across the line (the filler baseline) and treat tokens with large robust z-scores as the stored exceptions.
mechanism: Compute m = median over tokens, per dimension, of X (7 of 10 tokens are filler, so m ≈ the filler frame). Set D = (X − m)/(MAD + ε), where MAD is the per-dimension median absolute deviation. Exception score e_i = ||D_i||₂, gate g_i = sigmoid(a(e_i − b)) with learned a and b, and weights w_i = g_i·softmax_i(v·D_i). The key reads Σ w_i·W_k D_i and the value reads Σ w_i·W_v D_i. Because the baseline is removed, leaked filler content does not dilute the key and the content tokens sit in a clean residual frame. Params are about 2k. This is an order-statistic baseline, not a mean or max pool.
why_novel_names: An unseen name is still an outlier from the filler frame, with a large robust z-score, so it is gated in even though its direction is new. Gating is by deviation from a per-line baseline, not by similarity to a trained prototype.
nearest_known: Mean/max pooling and attention pooling with LayerNorm/whitening of keys. The difference is a per-line robust median baseline and MAD scaling, with an exception gate, as in patched frame-of-reference compression. The gate is not a learned similarity to training names.
prediction: Person weight at the value token (the leak) drops. Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 6 points and novel accuracy rises by about +0.04 to +0.05.
lens: databases: how a key is formed when the key value has never been seen

core_operation: Locate content tokens with a Foote checkerboard-kernel novelty curve computed on the line's 10x10 token self-similarity matrix, and use that curve plus off-diagonal similarity profiles as name-independent features for choosing the person token.
mechanism: Project the states to 16 dimensions: z_t = W h_t, then normalize each z_t to unit length. Compute S = Z Z^T (10x10). Novelty curve: n_t = sum over offsets a,b in {-2..2} of K[a,b] * S[t+a, t+b], with a learned 5x5 kernel K initialized to a checkerboard. Also take each token's sorted similarity row s_t (10 values, sorting removes position). Person score: p_t = MLP([n_t, s_t, ||h_t||]), with about 600 parameters. Softmax over p_t gives weights w. Key = A (sum_t w_t h_t) + B r, where r is a relation pool with its own score of the same kind. Value comes from a separate pool driven by the same features. All parameters are well under 20k. Train end-to-end with answer cross-entropy.
why_novel_names: The scores depend only on similarity structure: how unlike its neighbours a token is, and how leak traces couple it to other tokens. They never use the direction of the name vector, so an unseen name gets the same evidence as a seen one.
nearest_known: Foote (2000) audio novelty detection, and self-attention-then-pool. The difference is that the scoring is a fixed-geometry checkerboard convolution along the SSM diagonal plus sorted similarity rows, with no attention mixing of values.
prediction: Novel-name person-lost errors fall from 43% to about 25%; novel accuracy rises to about 0.70.

core_operation: Score each token for 'person-ness' with a quadrature-pair energy detector, the sum of squared responses of a small learned filter bank, so that role evidence is invariant to rotations within a subspace.
mechanism: For role r (person, relation, value), learn U_r, a 32x4 matrix. The energy is e_{r,t} = ||U_r^T h_t||^2 minus a learned bias. The person score is opponent energy: p_t = e_{P,t} - lambda * e_{V,t} - mu * e_{R,t}. Softmax over t gives w. Key = Wk [sum_t w_t h_t ; relation-pool], where the relation pool is built the same way. Value comes from a separate energy-weighted pool. Encourage each U_r to be orthonormal with a soft penalty, so the detector behaves like a complex cell (phase/sign-invariant). This uses about 3.5k parameters.
why_novel_names: A linear score w·h is driven partly by the random component of each name's vector, and that component is unseen for novel names. A subspace energy responds to any vector lying in the 'name-role' subspace regardless of its orientation within it. Novel names therefore trigger the detector as reliably as trained ones.
nearest_known: Single softmax attention pool with a linear scorer. The difference is that the scorer is a quadratic energy over a learned subspace with opponent channels, not a dot product. It is also not bilinear pooling, because nothing is pooled as an outer product.
prediction: The gap between familiar and novel person-selection accuracy shrinks. Novel accuracy is about 0.68, and person-lost errors fall to about 30%.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Use a CFAR (constant false alarm rate) detector: each token's person score is normalized by the mean and spread of the scores of background cells, excluding guard cells next to the candidate.
mechanism: Compute the raw score q_t = MLP(h_t) with about 2k parameters. For each t, the background set is all positions except t-1, t and t+1 (the guard cells). Background mean m_t and robust spread s_t are a trimmed mean and mean absolute deviation over that set. Detection statistic: d_t = (q_t - m_t)/(s_t + eps). Weights w = softmax(d_t). The key is built from the w-pooled state and a relation pool computed the same way. The value pool uses its own CFAR statistic. The guard cells keep the leakage that the reader spreads onto neighbours from inflating the background.
why_novel_names: An unseen name shifts the whole score profile of the line, for example by giving a lower absolute response. Standardizing against that line's own background turns detection into 'which token stands out here'. This decision stays stable under the distribution shift caused by unseen name vectors.
nearest_known: Temperature or entropy tricks on pool weights. The difference is a per-candidate, leave-guard-out background normalization (radar cell-averaging CFAR), not a global scaling of the logits.
prediction: Novel accuracy rises to about 0.66. Person-lost errors drop to about 32%, with the biggest gain on lines where the person is adjacent to the value.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Apply a learned inverse (Wiener-style) leak filter at the attended position: subtract the selected token's attention-weighted neighbour states, scaled by learned scalars, to undo the reader's mixing before writing the key.
mechanism: Pool weights w_t come from a standard scorer. The cleaned state at each t is c_t = h_t - a*h_{t-1} - b*h_{t+1} + g*(h_{t-2}+h_{t+2}), with three learned scalars initialized from a truncated series inverse of the mixing kernel. Person vector = sum_t w_t c_t. The same operation is applied to the relation pool. Key = Wk [person; relation], then normalized. The value uses an uncleaned pool, because the leaked person trace there is harmless. The filter is tied across dimensions, so it cannot store name structure.
why_novel_names: For a novel name, the person state's own component is weak and unfamiliar. The leaked relation and value content from neighbours then dominates the key's direction, so the cosine matches the wrong person's card. Deconvolution removes the neighbour contribution regardless of identity, leaving mostly the name vector, which the question's name vector can match.
nearest_known: Conv line encoders. The difference is a 3-scalar, dimension-tied inverse filter of the known mixing structure, applied only to produce the key. It is not a learned feature-extracting convolution.
prediction: Key-to-question cosine for the correct card rises on novel names. Person-lost errors fall from 43% to about 28%.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Do robust background subtraction: estimate the filler background as a per-dimension median across the 10 tokens, and build the key from rectified residuals (the contrast signal) rather than from raw states.
mechanism: Compute med = per-dimension median over the 10 states. With 3 content tokens and 7 fillers, the median tracks the background. Residual: u_t = h_t - med. Half-wave rectified contrast: v_t = [ReLU(u_t); ReLU(-u_t)], which is 64-dimensional. Person score: p_t = MLP(v_t). The relation score is computed the same way. The key is built from the pools of u_t, not of h_t, so the shared reader bias and filler content do not enter the key. The value uses its own pool of u_t. This uses about 8k parameters.
why_novel_names: Raw states of an unseen name carry a large common-mode component shared with fillers and the reader bias. That component makes keys look alike across people, so the cosine fails to separate them. Subtracting a robust line-specific background leaves the name-specific deviation, which the question's novel name vector can align with, without learning anything about names.
nearest_known: Mean pooling and LayerNorm/whitening of keys. The difference is a per-line median across tokens (a robust background estimator from image and audio onset detection), subtracted before scoring and pooling. It is not a normalization over feature dimensions.
prediction: Novel accuracy rises to about 0.65. Person-lost errors fall to about 33%, with familiar accuracy unchanged.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Run a few Euler steps of generalized Lotka-Volterra competition among the 10 tokens, using a learned signed, asymmetric interaction matrix computed from state geometry. Use the unnormalised surviving abundances as pooling weights.
mechanism: Project states p_i = W s_i (32->16). Interaction a_ij = tanh(p_i^T M p_j), with M 16x16. Set the carrying capacity from a linear score k_i = u.s_i. Start with n_i = 0.3. For t = 1..6, compute n_i <- relu(n_i + 0.3*n_i*(k_i - n_i - sum_j a_ij*n_j)). The 7 mutually similar fillers have large positive a_ij and exclude one another down to near 0. The 3 content tokens sit in sparse niches and persist. Key = sum_i n_i*Wk s_i, value = sum_i n_i*Wv s_i. Weights are not sum-to-one, so abundance is a population size rather than a share. Roughly 2k parameters.
why_novel_names: Survival depends on crowding geometry (is the token redundant with the others in the line?) and not on recognising a name. A novel name token is still isolated from the filler cloud, so it survives. A softmax scorer trained on 16 names can instead give a novel name a low logit.
nearest_known: Slot attention / softmax pooling competition. The difference is that competition is dynamical, pairwise and signed among the inputs themselves (token vs token), with extinction to zero and no normalisation across tokens.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to about 33%. Novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.64.

core_operation: Admixture-style donor analysis within the line. Express each token's state as a simplex-weighted mixture of the other tokens' states, then pool by net donation (donated minus received ancestry).
mechanism: p_i = W s_i (32->24), rows L2-normalised. For each i, find q_i on the simplex over j != i that minimises ||p_i - sum_j q_ij p_j||^2, using 5 unrolled exponentiated-gradient steps (step size learned). Compute the explained fraction e_i = 1 - residual/||p_i||^2. Net donor score d_j = sum_i e_i*(q_ij - q_ji). The antisymmetric form cancels mutual filler-filler explanation. A token whose trace leaks into the value token's state (via the neighbour mixing) is a net donor. Pool weights = softmax(g*d_j + c_j), with c_j a small linear score. Key = weighted sum through Wk, value through Wv. About 3k parameters.
why_novel_names: The person's trace in other states is explained by the person token's own state in the same line. No vocabulary is needed, so an unseen name vector still shows up as a donor.
nearest_known: Self-expressive subspace clustering / ridge-leverage pools. The difference is the directed, simplex-constrained, antisymmetrised donor flow (who contaminates whom), not a hat-matrix diagonal or a subspace residual.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from 43% to about 30%. Familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.97.

core_operation: Hybridisation-based speciation of names during training. Each step makes a fresh population of pseudo-novel names by blending and perturbing the 16 training name vectors, pushed through the frozen reader and answerer. The population turns over every batch.
mechanism: The writer is unchanged. In the training loop, for each visit, draw name vectors n = normalize(a*n_x + (1-a)*n_y + s*xi), with a~U(-0.3,1.3) (allows extrapolation), xi Gaussian, s~U(0,0.5). Use the same synthetic vector for that person in the lines and in the question. Run the lines through the frozen reader (including the neighbour mixing) and train with answer-only CE. A fresh set of names each batch means a rule that keys on the identity of one of the 16 names has no stable fitness. Only a rule that locates the person by structure survives. Optionally keep 25% pure familiar names.
why_novel_names: The writer sees a continuum of effectively novel names, so the learned person-finder must work off line structure and cannot memorise 16 points.
nearest_known: Mixup, and name-embedding augmentation in general. The difference is that blends are made at the token-vector level before the frozen reader, so mixing and context are regenerated consistently, and the population is resampled every step (Red Queen turnover).
prediction: Novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.68, and person-lost errors fall to about 27%. Familiar accuracy drops by 0.01 or less.
lens: evolution and ecology

core_operation: Null-model-corrected modularity eigenvectors of the within-line token affinity graph (ecological network modularity). Their coordinates feed the key and value heads.
mechanism: p_i = W s_i (32->16), A_ij = relu(cos(p_i,p_j)), zero diagonal. Degree k = A1 and total 2m = sum A. Modularity matrix B = A - k k^T/(2m), the configuration-model null. Shift B by cI, then power-iterate 8 steps with deflation to get the top 2 eigenvectors v1, v2. Fix sign so the sum over tokens is negative. Each token gets the coordinate vector c_i = (v1_i, v2_i, k_i/2m). Pool weights = softmax(w.[c_i, s_i-score]). Key = sum_i alpha_i*Wk s_i, value = sum_i alpha_i*Wv s_i. About 2.5k parameters. The null model removes the pull of the large, mutually similar filler clique.
why_novel_names: Group membership comes from relative affinities inside the line after subtracting what degree alone would predict. This does not depend on whether the name's vector was seen.
nearest_known: Covariance/bilinear pooling and spectral clustering. The difference is that the eigenvectors come from a degree-null-corrected, thresholded affinity graph, and eigen-coordinates replace pooled covariance statistics.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from 43% to about 35%. Novel accuracy rises to about 0.62.
lens: evolution and ecology

core_operation: Allopatric island training with a gradient-agreement mask. Split the 16 training names into islands, and update a writer parameter only where island gradients agree, with an inner-step held-out-island loss.
mechanism: Partition the training names into 4 islands of 4. Each step, draw one batch per island. Compute the gradients g_1..g_4 of the answer-CE for the full writer, which is any base writer such as the seed pool. Add a meta term, the loss on island B after one inner SGD step on island A (first-order, MLDG-style). Final update = mean(g) * mask, where mask_k = 1 if at least 3 of 4 islands share the sign of g_k (otherwise 0, or a soft sigmoid of the agreement). Re-draw the islands every epoch (migration). Parameters whose usefulness depends on specific names get no consistent gradient and are frozen. Parameters that find the person by line structure receive consistent gradients and are kept. This adds no inference-time parameters.
why_novel_names: Each island plays the role of unseen names for the others. The selection pressure rewards rules that transfer across name sets.
nearest_known: AND-mask / IRM / MLDG domain generalisation. The difference is that the environments are partitions of the person-name vocabulary, re-drawn each epoch, and the agreement mask is applied per parameter inside a pooling writer. No known item from the banned list uses it.
prediction: Gap between familiar and novel accuracy shrinks from 0.41 to about 0.28 (novel about 0.66). Person-lost errors fall to about 30%.
lens: evolution and ecology

core_operation: Run a typestate automaton with an exactly-once constraint over the 10 tokens, so each token is tagged filler, person, relation or value and each of the last three is used once, and take the forward-backward marginals as the selection weights.
mechanism: Each token gets tag scores e_t[F,P,R,V] = W s_t + b (a 32x4 matrix). The automaton state is the 3-bit set of {P,R,V} already consumed, which gives 8 states. A token tagged F keeps the state. A token tagged P, R or V is legal only if that bit is unset, and it sets the bit. The only accepted path ends in state 111. Run log-space forward-backward over 10 steps x 8 states. This yields marginals m_t(P), m_t(R) and m_t(V), and the cost is trivial. Then key = Wk [Σ m_t(P) s_t ; Σ m_t(R) s_t] (16 outputs) and value = Wv Σ m_t(V) s_t. Everything is trained by answer-only cross-entropy. There are fewer than 1,000 parameters.
why_novel_names: The relation and value tokens are known and are claimed confidently. The partition function still requires one P somewhere, so the leftover token gets the person mass even when its emission score is weak and unseen. The decision is made by exclusion with no threshold on the name's own score.
nearest_known: Structured attention with a linear-chain CRF (Kim et al. 2017), and slot attention. The difference is that the chain is a constrained exactly-once typestate automaton whose marginals replace softmax pooling weights. It has no slots, no iteration and no recurrent update.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to about 25%, and novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.70. Familiar accuracy stays at about 0.97 or above.
lens: compilers: type inference for an unseen identifier

core_operation: Invert the known neighbour-mixing operator on the token axis by a few contractive fixed-point (Neumann-series) iterations, so the person trace smeared onto neighbouring tokens is un-mixed before any selection.
mechanism: Model the reader as s = (I + M) c, where c is the clean token content and M mixes tokens at offsets ±1 and ±2 through scalar taps a_d and a channel matrix B (32x32, spectral norm constrained below 1). Initialise h0 = s. Iterate h_{k+1} = s - Σ_d a_d shift_d(h_k) B for k = 1..3. This is shared across all positions and uses no token identity. The learned operator is an approximate inverse of the mixing. Then build the key as a single linear readout, Wk [Σ w_t h_t ; Σ w'_t h_t], with simple softmax weights on h. Parameters are about 1,100 plus the readouts. The point is the un-mixing, not the pooling.
why_novel_names: The mixing operator is the same for every token vector, so its inverse is name-independent. Un-mixing removes neighbour contamination from the person token, and it removes the smeared person component from the value token. That clean separation does not need the name's identity to have been seen.
nearest_known: Conv/GRU line encoders, and Deep Equilibrium models. The difference is that this is a constrained inverse of a known linear mixing, solved as a dataflow-style fixpoint with a contraction guarantee. It is not a general learned encoder layer.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 8 points, from 43% to about 35%. A linear probe on the un-mixed states should find the person position on novel names above 99%.
lens: compilers: type inference for an unseen identifier

core_operation: Put the line in canonical form with a differentiable sort by a learned scalar type-rank, then read key and value from fixed rank slots of the sorted sequence.
mechanism: Compute the scalar r_t = u·s_t + c. Apply NeuralSort or a soft permutation P with temperature τ to get a 10x32 canonical sequence C = P S, ordered by descending r. Use separate readouts per rank slot: key = Σ_{j=1..4} Wk_j C_j, and value = Σ_{j=1..4} Wv_j C_j. The learned u should put the relation and value tokens at the top and the fillers at the bottom, leaving the person in the middle band. Positions in the line are random, so the sort removes that nuisance variable. Only the top 4 slots have readouts. Parameters are about 4*(16+32)*32 = 6k, plus u.
why_novel_names: Slot assignment depends on order relations, not absolute scores. An unseen name only has to score above the filler band and below the known relation and value band. Its exact score is irrelevant, unlike with a threshold or a softmax weight.
nearest_known: SortPooling in graph nets, and NeuralSort. The difference is the use of rank-indexed slot readouts as a canonical-form pass that normalises position. It is not a pooling over sorted features by a single shared head.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall to about 32%. Novel accuracy is about 0.65, with a small drop in familiar accuracy (about 0.96).
lens: compilers: type inference for an unseen identifier

core_operation: Give each token a name-agnostic geometric signature, namely the sorted profile of its cosines to the other 9 tokens (a soft value-numbering or common-subexpression signature), and score person-ness from that signature only.
mechanism: Compute the cosine matrix G (10x10) of the states. Take the row-sorted profile p_t = sort_desc(G_t,≠t), together with ‖s_t‖ and the cosine to the two positional neighbours. Score q_t = MLP(p_t, ‖s_t‖) with 10 inputs, 16 hidden units and 3 tag logits (filler, person-or-relation-or-value, and so on). Because filler tokens repeat, they have a high-cosine twin in the line. Content tokens are unique, so their profile is flat. A second head on a pair signature (cosine to the other two content candidates) splits the person from the relation and value. Selection weights come from softmax(q); key and value are linear readouts of the weighted state sums. The signature features are coordinate-free, and the content readout is the only place the 32-d coordinates are used. Parameters: about 1k.
why_novel_names: The score never looks at which direction a name has. It sees only whether the token is unique and how it relates geometrically to the rest of the line. A novel name vector has the same uniqueness signature as a trained name.
nearest_known: Relation networks and bilinear/covariance pooling, which pool pairwise terms into the content. The difference is that the Gram matrix is used only as a sorted per-row descriptor for scoring, and its values never enter the key or value. It resembles hash-consing / value numbering in compilers.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 10 points, to about 33%. The gain depends on fillers repeating. If the filler vocabulary is large the gain shrinks to 2 to 3 points.
lens: compilers: type inference for an unseen identifier

core_operation: Lower the selected state to the key by an orthogonal (Cayley-parameterised) change of basis followed by a frozen random slice, so the key map is an isometry that cannot discard name directions unseen in training.
mechanism: Weights for selecting tokens come from any standard scorer. Compute the pooled person estimate z (32-d). Compute the key as k = J Q z, where Q = (I-A)(I+A)^-1 is orthogonal and A is a learned skew-symmetric 32x32 matrix. J is a frozen random 16x32 slice with orthonormal rows. The relation part of the key goes through a separate Q' in the same way, and the two are summed to give 16 dims. The value path is a plain linear map. With only 16 seen names the key map is determined on a 16-d subspace. The orthogonality constraint fixes the completion on the other 16 dims so that novel name directions keep their norm and angles, instead of being collapsed by an overfitted rank-16 map. Parameters: about 1,000 for A.
why_novel_names: A novel name differs from the seen names mostly in directions that an unconstrained map was never penalised for collapsing. An isometric lowering preserves the distinctness of any two unseen names, so cosine matching against the question stays discriminative between persons.
nearest_known: LayerNorm/whitening of keys, and orthogonal RNN weights. The difference is a hard isometry constraint on the write map itself (a lossless lowering), with a frozen slice for compression. It is not a normalisation of the key statistics.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 5 points, to about 38%, because only the collapse failure mode is addressed. Familiar accuracy is unchanged within 1 point.
lens: compilers: type inference for an unseen identifier

core_operation: Ordered-statistic CFAR (radar constant-false-alarm-rate) detection: each token's learned-subspace energy is divided by a trimmed leave-one-out estimate of the line's own clutter level, and tokens are kept by an un-normalised sigmoid threshold instead of a softmax.
mechanism: Project each token with P (32→8) and take e_i = ||P h_i||². For token i, the clutter c_i is the k-th ranked energy among the other 9 tokens, with k learned through a soft rank interpolation. This excludes the guard cells, i.e. the other content tokens, which are the largest energies. Compute the detection weight a_i = sigmoid(g·(log e_i − log c_i) − b). Do not normalise the a_i, so a line with three content tokens yields about three active weights. Key = Wk(Σ a_i h_i)/(Σ a_i+ε), mapping 32→16. Value = Wv(Σ a_i h_i) with Wv 32→32. Parameters: P, g, b, k, Wk, Wv, about 2k numbers in total.
why_novel_names: The decision rests on a ratio to the line's own background, not on an absolute score tuned to the 16 training name vectors. A novel name that merely stands out from the filler (e.g. a smaller norm in P) is still detected, so its weight does not collapse the way a memorised softmax logit can.
nearest_known: Single softmax attention pool with temperature/entropy tricks. The difference is a per-token adaptive threshold from leave-one-out rank statistics with no sum-to-one constraint, so the number of detections is not forced.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to about 33%. Novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.65 with familiar accuracy at least 0.96.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Robust background subtraction with a learned L-filter (order-statistic filter): for each channel, sort the 10 token values, take a learned linear combination of the sorted ranks as the clutter map, and subtract it from every token before any pooling.
mechanism: For each of the 32 channels, sort the 10 values across tokens to get r_1..r_10. Compute the background b_c = Σ_k w_k r_k, with 10 weights w shared over channels and initialised to a median bump at ranks 5–6. Residual tokens are d_i = h_i − b. Because 7 of 10 tokens are filler, the background approximates the filler state and the residuals carry the three content tokens. Then apply a single linear read-out. Key = Wk(Σ_i softmax(q·d_i) d_i). Value = Wv(same pooled vector). The only new parameters are the 10 order-statistic weights, plus Wk and Wv.
why_novel_names: The subtraction is computed from the line itself, so it removes common-mode content (filler, positional offsets, reader bias) with no dependence on name identity. The residual of an unseen name token keeps its full amplitude and is not hidden by features that were fitted to the training names.
nearest_known: Mean/max pooling and LayerNorm/whitening of keys. The difference is a rank-based per-channel baseline that is subtracted per token before attention. It is neither a normalisation of the output nor a learned pool of the tokens.
prediction: Novel-name accuracy rises by about 0.05–0.08. The person-lost share falls to about 35%, and the gain is largest on lines where the person token sits at the edge of the line.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Canny-style double-threshold hysteresis along the token axis: strong content detections seed, and weak candidates are admitted only if they are adjacent to a strong one, which exploits the neighbour-mixing leakage as an edge-linking cue.
mechanism: Compute a scalar contrast score z_i = u·h_i − mean over a window of ±2 tokens (centre-surround). Compute s_i = sigmoid(α(z_i − T_hi)) and w_i = sigmoid(α(z_i − T_lo)), with T_hi > T_lo learned. Link: m_i = max(s_i, w_i · max(s_{i−1}, s_{i+1})). Using positions as the axis is legitimate because the mixing is positional. Pool p = Σ m_i h_i / (Σ m_i+ε) and produce the key and value with two linear maps Wk and Wv. Total parameters: u, T_hi, T_lo, α, Wk, Wv.
why_novel_names: A person name next to the relation or value token has only a weak or ambiguous score on its own, which is what happens with novel vectors. The link step recovers it from the strong neighbour, so recovery does not depend on knowing that name's vector.
nearest_known: Top-k / sparsemax hard token selection, and conv line encoders. The difference is two-level thresholding with connectivity (a hysteresis-linking operation) that is not a softmax or a top-k and not a learned convolution.
prediction: On novel names the person-lost errors drop from about 43% to about 36%, concentrated in lines where the person token is adjacent to another content token. Accuracy for non-adjacent lines is unchanged.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Tied-tap Wiener inverse filtering along the token axis: undo the neighbour mixing with a 3-tap symmetric deconvolution shared across all 32 channels before any selection, so each token state is sharpened towards its own token identity.
mechanism: Parametrise the mixing as a circulant or banded operator M = I + a(S+S^T), with S the 10×10 shift matrix, using one scalar a. Learn the Wiener gain 1/(1 + a·cos ω_k) with a noise-to-signal regulariser λ per DFT bin. Equivalently, apply the 10×10 matrix G = (M^T M + λI)^{-1} M^T to the state matrix H (10×32), giving H' = G H. Only a and λ are trainable, 2 numbers. Then pool H' with the existing seed softmax pool. Key = Wk(pool), value = Wv(pool). The aim is that the person token's own vector, not its smeared trace on the value token, determines the key.
why_novel_names: The deconvolution is token-identity-free and shared across channels, so it cannot memorise names. It removes the leakage that makes a novel person look like a value token or a relation token, so the pooled key carries the person content cleanly.
nearest_known: GRU/LSTM/conv line encoders. The difference is an inverse (deconvolution) operator with 2 physical parameters, fixed in structure by the mixing model, not a learned general conv kernel with many parameters.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 6 points, to about 37%. Familiar accuracy is unchanged within ±0.01.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Square-law log-filterbank energy detection (mel/cepstral-style): describe each token by log-energies in a small learned bank of 8 filters, and discard sign and orientation, so that a token's class is decided from subspace energy rather than from vector direction.
mechanism: Learn W (8×32). Compute f_i = log(ε + (W h_i)²), 8 values per token, with log compression as in mel features. Score tokens with a small linear read-out s_i = v·f_i, then standardise s over the line's 10 tokens by z-score. Attention weights = softmax(γ·z_i). Pool the original states h_i with these weights and compute the key and value with Wk and Wv. Optionally add the pooled f_i vector to the key, which gives a phase-invariant person descriptor. The parameter count is about 8·32 + 8 + 2 + Wk + Wv, under 3k.
why_novel_names: Training names occupy a person subspace, whereas their directions within it differ. Square-law energy responds to being in that subspace and is unaffected by which direction within it a particular name takes. A novel name lies in the same subspace, so its score is high, whereas a linear score is tied to the sign and direction of the 16 seen names.
nearest_known: Bilinear/covariance pooling and GeM. The difference is that the quadratic energy features are used only for selection, through a log-compressed filterbank. Pooling is not done over second-order statistics.
prediction: Novel accuracy goes from 0.57 to about 0.66, and the gap between familiar and novel accuracy shrinks from about 0.41 to about 0.30. If it does not help, the person-lost share on novel names stays near 43%, which would show that the person subspace is not energy-separable.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Break the router/payload symmetry: the token-selection network sees a copy of the line whose states are pushed along adversarially learned directions, while the key and value are pooled from the clean states with those weights.
mechanism: Router r = MLP 32→64→1, applied per token. During training, form x̃_t = x_t + σ·U ε_t, where U is 32×4 with unit columns and ε_t ~ N(0, I) is drawn independently for each token. U is trained through a gradient-reversal layer, so it moves to maximize the answer cross-entropy. σ is annealed up to about the norm of a single name component. Pool weights a = softmax(r(x̃)/τ). Key = W_k Σ a_t x_t (16×32) and value = W_v Σ b_t x_t (b from a second router that sees the clean states). Only routing gradients see the perturbation, so the adversary can only attack WHERE the writer looks, not WHAT it stores. At test time σ = 0. About 5k numbers.
why_novel_names: The cheapest routing rule on 16 names is a name-specific detector. The adversary finds and shakes the directions such a detector relies on, which forces a person-locator that depends on role-level structure. That is the structure that carries over to unseen name vectors.
nearest_known: Adversarial data augmentation / gradient-reversal (DANN). Difference: the perturbation is applied only to the router's view and never to the stored payload, and it is per-token noise in a learned low-rank subspace rather than input-level augmentation or domain labels.
prediction: Novel-name person-lost errors drop from about 43% to about 30%; familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.96.
lens: physics: symmetry breaking and conserved quantities

core_operation: Role-charge conservation: the person weight has no detector of its own and is defined as the conserved content charge (exactly 3 per line) minus the relation charge and the value charge.
why_novel_names: Each head that has parameters judges a closed, fully familiar class, so it generalizes to new lines. An unseen name never has to be recognized: it inherits the charge left over by exclusion. The person locator therefore contains no name-dependent parameters at all.
nearest_known: Two separate pools / role-specific projections (type-aware pooling). Difference: there is no person pool; the person weight is a parameter-free conservation residual of the other charges, not a learned projection.
prediction: Novel-name accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.72; the person-lost share falls to about 25%.
lens: physics: symmetry breaking and conserved quantities

core_operation: Make the router invariant under a learned block-sign symmetry group {±1}^8, so its input features are block energies, not signed name patterns.
mechanism: Learn an orthogonal Q = exp(A − Aᵀ) (32×32) and split Qx into 8 blocks of 4. The router's features per token are block energies e_b = ||Q_b x||² plus all pairwise block-norm products, all invariant to flipping the sign of any block. Router MLP: 36 features → 32 → 1, then softmax over tokens for the person and relation pools; a separate pool picks the value. Key and value are linear maps of the clean signed pooled states: key 16×64, value 32×32. About 3.5k numbers.
why_novel_names: Each familiar name is effectively expanded to its 256-element sign orbit. The router cannot memorize the signed direction of 16 names; it must use energy distribution across learned subspaces. Random novel name vectors share that distribution with familiar ones while differing in sign pattern.
nearest_known: SignNet (Lim et al. 2022), which gives sign invariance for eigenvectors. Difference: the blocks are a learned partition used to erase token identity from a pooling router, whereas SignNet uses a fixed eigenvector sign ambiguity.
prediction: The novel-name person-lost share drops from 43% to about 32%, at a cost of about 1 point of familiar accuracy.
lens: physics: symmetry breaking and conserved quantities

core_operation: Conserve rank in the person-to-key map by parameterizing it with a bounded singular spectrum, so directions unseen in training cannot be annihilated.
mechanism: Key = U·diag(s)·Vᵀ·p, where p is the pooled person/relation state (64-dim). U (16×16) and V (64×16) are orthonormal via a Cayley/QR parameterization, and s = 0.5 + 1.5·sigmoid(θ), so all gains lie in [0.5, 2]. Add a separate unconstrained relation component on fixed key coordinates 13–16. The value map is unconstrained. There is no bias, keeping the key linear-homogeneous in p. Use the seed attention pool for p. About 3k numbers.
why_novel_names: A free W fitted on 16 names only learns gains inside their ≤16-dimensional span. Novel names point partly outside it, so their key component shrinks and cosine scoring is then dominated by the relation part, which lets decoys win. Bounded spectrum is a norm-conservation law: every input direction keeps at least half its energy into the key.
nearest_known: Orthogonal/unitary RNN parameterizations, and the listed LayerNorm/whitening of keys. Difference: this constrains the writer's linear map itself to a bounded condition number, rather than normalizing outputs.
prediction: The novel-name cosine margin between the correct card and the decoy rises by about 0.1; novel-name accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.65.
lens: physics: symmetry breaking and conserved quantities

core_operation: Canonicalize each token in the line's own reference frame, built from the familiar relation and value anchors, and route only on rotation-invariant Gram coordinates in that frame.
why_novel_names: Under neighbour mixing, the person token carries traces of the relation and value. In the frame these show up as specific in-frame coordinates, a familiar signature regardless of the name. Rotating the name component leaves every router feature unchanged, so the router cannot depend on name identity.
nearest_known: Frame averaging / canonicalization (Puny et al. 2022). Difference: the frame is built per line from learned soft anchors on familiar roles, and only within-frame invariants drive a pooling router, rather than a global symmetry group frame for equivariant networks.
prediction: The novel-name person-lost share falls from 43% to about 22%; novel accuracy reaches about 0.75.
lens: physics: symmetry breaking and conserved quantities

core_operation: Choose the person token with a scorer whose only inputs are a few per-token summary statistics, like a database zone map, and never the raw 32-number state, so the scorer cannot represent name identity.
mechanism: For each token t compute a statistics vector s_t of about 8 numbers: L2 norm, max |x|, kurtosis across the 32 dims, cosine to the line mean, cosine to the line's top principal direction, norm of the residual after removing the line mean, rank of the norm within the line, and the entropy of softmax(x). A tiny MLP (8-16-1, about 160 params) maps s_t to a score. Softmax over the 10 tokens gives weights w. The key is W_k(sum w_t x_t) with W_k of size 32x16. The value comes from a separate small learned pool, W_v times a pool, 32x32. Train end-to-end on answer cross-entropy. There is no per-dimension access in the scorer.
why_novel_names: An unseen name's vector is new, but its role signature is not. Mixing pattern, norm profile and distance from the line centroid come from the reader's structure. A scorer that sees only these invariants cannot store which 16 names were in training.
nearest_known: Single softmax attention pool (seed). Difference: the score function's input is a fixed set of statistics invariant to dimension permutation, not a learned projection of the state. This removes the capacity to encode name identity.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to 20-25%; novel accuracy rises to about 0.70; familiar accuracy drops by 0.02 at most.
lens: databases: how a key is formed when the key value has never been seen

core_operation: Score each token by its sorted similarity profile to the other 9 tokens, the way blocking keys work in record linkage, instead of by its own content.
mechanism: Compute the 10x10 cosine Gram matrix G of the reader states, using a learned 32x32 metric M so that G_ij = cos(Mx_i, Mx_j). For token i, sort row i without the diagonal in descending order to get a 9-vector. Append the sorted row of the same matrix computed with the raw identity metric, giving 18 numbers. An MLP (18-32-1) gives the score, and a softmax over tokens gives person weights. The key is W_k(sum w x). A second profile-MLP head gives value weights, and the value is W_v(sum u x). Total is about 3k params.
why_novel_names: Neighbour mixing gives the person token a characteristic similarity pattern to the relation and value tokens. Sorting removes position, and the profile is relational, so the sorted profile has the same shape whichever name occupies the slot. The selector reads only a relational shape, never name coordinates.
nearest_known: Relation networks (pairwise, then sum). Difference: there is no summed pairwise embedding. The per-token sorted similarity row is used only as a selection score, and the pooled content stays the raw token state.
prediction: Novel-name accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.72; person-lost errors fall to about 22%.
lens: databases: how a key is formed when the key value has never been seen

core_operation: Form the key from the token at a fixed ordinal position among the content tokens, the way a composite key is defined by column order rather than column value, using a soft prefix count of content-ness.
mechanism: A content detector c_t = sigmoid(a·x_t + b) is trained jointly. Its targets are implicit: fillers are a closed, seen class, so the detector generalises. Compute the soft prefix count P_t = sum_{s<t} c_s. Learn three ordinal selectors. The first-content weight is w_t = c_t·exp(-P_t^2/τ), normalised; the second and third use (P_t-1)^2 and (P_t-2)^2. A learned 3-way softmax mixture chooses which ordinal feeds the key, and another chooses which feeds the value. The key is W_k(pooled), 32x16; the value is W_v(pooled), 32x32. If the generator keeps the order (person, relation, value), the mixture locks onto ordinal 1 for the key.
why_novel_names: The selection uses only whether a token is content, which is learned from fillers that are all seen, and the token's rank among content tokens. Neither depends on the name vector, so an unseen name in the first content slot is picked exactly as a seen one is.
nearest_known: Role-specific projections (type-aware pooling) and positional attention. Difference: the pointer is an ordinal rank computed by a cumulative sum over a content mask, not an absolute position embedding or a role classifier.
prediction: If the order is preserved: novel accuracy above 0.85 and person-lost errors below 10%. If not: no gain, and the mixture weights reveal this within one epoch.
lens: databases: how a key is formed when the key value has never been seen

core_operation: Find the person by anti-join: the person weight is the product of the not-filler, not-relation and not-value probabilities. The person class gets no positive detector at all.
mechanism: Train three closed-class detectors on the 32-dim states, each a 32-16-1 MLP: filler f_t, relation r_t and value v_t. Fillers and the 4 relations are closed vocabularies seen in training, so these generalise. Person weight: p_t ∝ (1-f_t)(1-r_t)(1-v_t). Additionally enforce one relation and one value per line by softmax-normalising r and v over tokens before taking complements. The key is W_k(sum p x). The value is W_v(sum softmax(v) x). Train with answer cross-entropy only, plus an auxiliary loss requiring sum(1-f) ≈ 3 (three content tokens, which is known schema, not a label). Parameters: about 4k.
why_novel_names: Nothing in the person pathway is trained to recognise names. A novel name is selected because it is none of the closed classes the writer has fully seen. Exclusion by known types is how a database accepts an unseen key value.
nearest_known: Type-aware pooling and novelty-subspace pools. Difference: there is no learned person projection and no residual or novelty norm. Selection is the logical complement of exclusive closed-class memberships under a uniqueness constraint.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall to about 15%; novel accuracy rises to about 0.78.
lens: databases: how a key is formed when the key value has never been seen

core_operation: Constrain the key projection to be an isometry (orthonormal rows, kept on the Stiefel manifold), so that the key map preserves cosine geometry for names whose vectors were never seen, like an order-preserving encoding of unseen key values.
mechanism: Use any name-agnostic selector, for example the seed pool, with a 32-1 score. Parameterise the key projection as K = first 16 rows of the matrix exponential of A, exp(A), with A = S - S^T for a free 32x32 S. This keeps K's rows orthonormal (Stiefel manifold) throughout training. Key = K·pooled. No bias and no nonlinearity on the key path. The value projection W_v (32x32) is unconstrained. An optional learned scalar gain before the cosine is a no-op, since cosine is scale-free. About 2.1k params.
why_novel_names: An unconstrained key map trained on 16 names can collapse directions that separate unseen names, or warp them toward seen ones. An isometry cannot discard or warp any direction, so the angles between unseen name vectors survive into the keys, and cosine matching to the question remains discriminative.
nearest_known: LayerNorm or whitening of keys, and LSH keys. Difference: this is not a normalisation of key statistics and not a random hash. It is a hard geometric constraint on the learned map itself, which forbids name-specific distortion.
prediction: With the seed selector, person-lost errors on novel names fall from 43% to about 33%; familiar accuracy is unchanged.
lens: databases: how a key is formed when the key value has never been seen

core_operation: Entropy-constrained optimal-transport role assignment: tokens are sent to {person, relation, value, filler} by Sinkhorn with fixed column marginals (1,1,1,7), so the person is found by exclusion rather than by recognising the name.
mechanism: Score matrix S (10 tokens x 4 roles) = X·W with W a 32x4 linear map (128 parameters), plus a learned role bias. Run 5 to 8 Sinkhorn iterations on exp(S/tau) with row marginals 1/10 each and column marginals (1,1,1,7)/10. This gives a transport plan P. Relation and value tokens come from a small closed vocabulary, so their columns become sharp during training. Column normalisation then forces the one remaining content token into the person column, even when the person score itself is weak. Key = Linear16(sum_t P[t,person]·x_t ⊕ sum_t P[t,rel]·x_t). Value = Linear32(sum_t P[t,val]·x_t). Training is answer-only cross-entropy, and the plan is differentiable. About 3k parameters in total.
why_novel_names: The person column is defined by the counting constraint 'exactly one person per line'. The relation and value detectors do the recognising, and those vocabularies are seen in training. A novel name vector therefore only has to be 'the leftover content token', and no name identity is stored.
nearest_known: Slot attention and softmax attention pooling. The difference is that assignment uses a doubly-constrained transport plan with fixed role cardinalities (Sinkhorn, as in SwAV equipartition), not an independent softmax over slots or tokens.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to about 25%, giving novel accuracy of roughly 0.70 with familiar names staying at 0.97 or above.

core_operation: Escape-symbol coding (PPM / Good-Turing missing mass): each token's probability of being outside a learned dictionary of known symbols is transmitted as a literal copy of its state.
mechanism: Learn a dictionary D of 40 atoms (32-d) that covers fillers, relation tokens and value tokens. For each token, compute a soft assignment a_t = softmax over [-||x_t - d_k||²/s for k=1..40, and a constant escape logit e0]. The escape probability E_t is the last component, which is the PPM escape mass. Key = Linear16(sum_t E_t·x_t / (sum_t E_t + eps)), with a small second term for the relation. The relation comes from the soft-assigned atoms, using the usual pooling with a learned class prior on the relation atoms. Value = Linear32 of the value atoms' weighted state plus E-weighted literal. Only 4k parameters, and the escape constant is learned.
why_novel_names: A novel name vector is by construction far from every atom, so its escape mass is high with no knowledge of which name it is. It is transmitted as a literal (analog) copy. A familiar-name shortcut cannot be learned, because the dictionary is trained only to cover the closed vocabularies.
nearest_known: VQ codebook keys and the project's novelty-subspace pool. The difference is that the signal is a probability mass with an explicit escape outcome and a literal-copy branch (PPM/Good-Turing), not a subspace projection residual or a quantised key.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 8 points, to roughly 35%. Novel accuracy rises to about 0.63 and familiar accuracy slips by at most 0.01.

core_operation: Johnson-Lindenstrauss isometry prior on the person-content path: the map from state to key is constrained to be a near-orthogonal partial isometry, so geometry is preserved outside the 16-name training span.
mechanism: Use any gating or pooling to select the person content vector u (32-d), for example the seed attention pool. Then compute key = Q·u with Q (16x32) parametrised as the first 16 rows of a Cayley-transform orthogonal matrix, or as a free matrix with penalty lambda·||QQ^T - I||². Optionally add a learned positive scalar per key dimension only for the relation part, which keeps role-specific scaling away from the name part. The 16 training names span only a 16-d subspace of the 32-d state space, so an unconstrained linear map is undetermined on the other 16 directions, and novel names have components there. The orthogonality constraint fixes those directions to a distance-preserving choice, so cosine similarity between a question's name vector and the key stays faithful. About 600 parameters in the name path.
why_novel_names: Novel names fall partly outside the span of the 16 training names. An isometry keeps the angle between a novel name's question vector and its key close to the angle between the original token states, so the cosine readout still discriminates.
nearest_known: Orthogonal-weight regularisation and Johnson-Lindenstrauss random projection. This is not in the KNOWN list, which only has LSH keys and hypernetworks. The difference is that the constraint is placed on the content-to-key map because of the span deficit, rather than as a generic regulariser.
prediction: The share of novel-name errors attributable to the wrong card drops by about 6 points. Novel accuracy rises to about 0.62, with familiar accuracy unchanged to within 0.01.
lens: information theory: what is cheapest to transmit about a line

core_operation: Robust baseline delta coding: subtract the per-channel median across the line's 10 tokens (the common filler background) before any selection, and transmit only deviations.
mechanism: For each of the 32 channels, compute m_c = median over the 10 tokens. Then r_t = x_t - m (the median is a non-parametric differential reference; 7 of 10 tokens are filler, so the median approximates the filler state). Additionally divide each channel by its median absolute deviation (MAD) over the line. Feed r_t into the attention pool (query/key/value maps on r_t, no extra parameters beyond the seed's). Optionally concatenate the line-level scale vector MAD (32-d) into the value path. Median and MAD are permutation-invariant and cost zero parameters.
why_novel_names: Filler-dependent state and the mixing leak from neighbours are shared across tokens, and the median removes them for any name. The remaining deviation is large only for content tokens, so the pool's discrimination between content and filler does not depend on the identity of the name. The weak person trace left on neighbours is also cleaned.
nearest_known: LayerNorm/whitening of keys, and mean/max pooling. The difference is that the line's own robust median baseline is subtracted across tokens (order-statistic differential coding), not a per-token normalisation or a pooled statistic.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 5 points, to roughly 38%. Novel accuracy about 0.60.

core_operation: Multiple-description coding with token-erasure ensembles: the key is the average of K independently erased descriptions, so the writer must carry the person's identity redundantly.
mechanism: Define a base writer f (the seed attention pool with a small MLP). Draw K=3 random erasure masks that zero out 30% of the tokens (a different mask each time). Compute k_j = f(X ⊙ mask_j) for j=1..3, key = normalise(mean_j k_j), value likewise. At test time K is still 3 but with masks drawn from the same distribution (or with K=1 and no mask). The person identity is available in two places: the person token itself and the weak trace on its neighbours, so a description missing either must be rescued by the other. The writer learns to use both cues, and no single fragile feature (such as a memorised name direction) can carry the key. No extra parameters.
why_novel_names: A memorised per-name feature works only when that token is present and recognised. Under erasure, the writer is pushed to use name-agnostic cues (the trace on neighbours and positional co-occurrence with the relation and value tokens) that carry the person for any name, including a novel one.
nearest_known: Dropout/token dropout and multi-head pooling. The difference is that independently erased descriptions are averaged inside the key as a multiple-description code, so redundancy is part of the transmitted object and not only a training regulariser.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 4 points. Novel accuracy rises to about 0.60 and familiar accuracy drops by up to 0.01.

core_operation: Thymic education: the person-selection weights must stay the same when the selected token's content is swapped for a random never-seen vector drawn from the token distribution.
mechanism: Base writer is the seed: score_t = MLP(s_t), alpha = softmax(score), key = Wk·sum alpha_t s_t, and the value comes from the seed's value pool. During training, for each line take the argmax-alpha token t* (stop-gradient on the choice). Build a 'mutant line' by replacing s_t* with a draw from N(mu, Sigma), where mu and Sigma are running statistics of all token states. Add the loss lambda·KL(alpha_original || alpha_mutant), computed on the scorer only. The answer cross-entropy is computed on the original line only. This adds no label, because the consistency target is the model's own selection. Params: about 6k (scorer 32x64x1, Wk 512, Wv 1024). lambda is about 0.5 and is ramped up after warm-up.
why_novel_names: Clones that recognise the 16 training identities are deleted: the scorer is penalised whenever its choice depends on WHICH name vector sits there. It can only fire on cues a random unseen vector also triggers, such as not being vocabulary and the neighbour-mixing signature. That is the situation at test time.
nearest_known: Consistency regularisation (UDA, Xie 2020; token dropout). Difference: the substitution targets only the model's own selected slot, uses a fresh random content vector, and constrains selection invariance rather than prediction invariance.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to about 25%. Novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.70, and familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.96.
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: NK-cell missing-self detection: a token's selection score is ONLY how badly it fails to match every entry of a learned 'self' codebook, with no direct content scorer.
mechanism: Learn a codebook C of 96 vectors x 32 (3072 numbers). For each token, m_t = max_k cos(s_t, c_k) and score_t = -beta·m_t + b. The temperature beta is fixed at 8; b is a scalar. alpha = softmax(score_t) and key = Wk·sum alpha_t s_t. The value uses a separate standard pool (seed). The codebook never feeds keys or values; its only job is to absorb things to ignore. Answer cross-entropy alone shapes C, through this route: if a codebook entry drifts toward a training name, that name stops being selected and the loss rises, so gradient repels C from all name vectors. Meanwhile C must cover fillers, relations and values, which otherwise steal attention. Add a small diversity term (penalise pairwise cosine between codebook entries above 0.9). Total is about 4.6k numbers.
why_novel_names: The selector has no parameter that can encode a specific name. 'Person' is defined as whatever the self library does not cover. Relations, values and fillers are all familiar vocabulary, so an unseen name is uncovered by construction.
nearest_known: VQ codebook keys / novelty-subspace pools. Difference: the codebook is a pure exclusion set whose max-affinity defines the pool weight, and selection has no positive detector. It is not a subspace residual and is not used to form keys.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall to about 20%. Novel accuracy is about 0.73, with the familiar–novel gap shrinking below 0.25.
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: Peripheral anergy: an adversary tries to read the questioned person's identity out of the selector's hidden features, and gradient reversal makes the selector blind to identity while still selecting.
mechanism: The selector computes h_t = ReLU(A s_t) (A is 32x48), score_t = u·h_t, alpha = softmax(score_t). The key path uses the raw states, key = Wk·sum alpha_t s_t, so identity still reaches the key. The adversary is a training-only head, linear 48→16, that predicts the question vector's person component from sum alpha_t h_t. Its training target is the question vector the answerer already uses, so no new label is introduced. The adversary is placed behind a gradient-reversal layer (coefficient 0.3). The selector thus minimises answer cross-entropy while maximising the adversary's error. Total numbers are about 4k, and the adversary is discarded after training.
why_novel_names: The 'person detector' cannot use the identity features that make it fit 16 specific names. The only selection signal left is identity-free 'this is the person slot' evidence, which transfers to unseen tokens.
nearest_known: Domain-adversarial training (DANN, Ganin 2016). Difference: the nuisance is the entity identity itself, the reversal is confined to the selection pathway, and the content pathway is left identity-rich.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from 43% to about 28%. Familiar accuracy drops at most 0.02.
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: Kinetic proofreading: the final pool weight is the renormalised product of several selection softmaxes, each computed on a different fixed random masking of feature dimensions, so a token must win every independent check.
mechanism: Fix K=5 random binary masks M_k, each keeping 20 of 32 dimensions; they are drawn once and never trained. Stage k scores tokens with its own small scorer (a_k ∈ R^32, applied to M_k ⊙ s_t, plus a bias), giving p_k = softmax over the 10 tokens. The combined weight is alpha_t ∝ prod_k p_k(t)^(1/K), renormalised. key = Wk·sum alpha_t s_t; the value comes from the seed value pool. Each stage is also trained, with 0.2 weight, on an answer cross-entropy computed using its own p_k. This forces each stage to be competent alone, so the product is a true AND. Params: about 1.8k.
why_novel_names: Each training name can be memorised through accidental alignments in particular dimensions, and different masks hide different ones. The product suppresses selection that depends on such coincidences. It keeps the class-level person cue, which is spread across dimensions and is present in every mask, including for unseen names.
nearest_known: Product of Experts (Hinton 2002) and the random subspace method (Ho 1998). Neither is used as a token-selection AND over fixed dimension masks; this is not multi-head pooling, because heads are multiplied, not concatenated.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall to about 30%. Novel accuracy is about 0.66.
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: Innate pattern-recognition receptor: the person query is a non-discriminative consensus vector, a running centroid of the model's own selected-token states minus the centroid of all tokens, rather than a gradient-trained scorer.
mechanism: Maintain two exponential moving averages over training (decay 0.99). mu_all is the mean of all token states. mu_sel is the mean of sum_t alpha_t s_t, i.e. the attention-weighted state each line selects. The receptor is r = normalise(mu_sel - mu_all). score_t = g·cos(s_t - mu_all, r) + v·s_t, where g is a learned gain and v is a tiny learned correction vector under heavy L2 decay (1e-2). alpha = softmax(score_t) and key = Wk·sum alpha_t s_t. Training warms up for 2 epochs with v free, then freezes v's norm budget at 0.1·g so the consensus receptor dominates. Params: about 1.6k plus 64 buffer numbers.
why_novel_names: A centroid over 16 names averages out each name's idiosyncratic direction (residual of about 1/4 each) and keeps the shared 'person-class' direction. That shared direction is what the 97% probe exploits on unseen names. A discriminative scorer instead fits each name's specifics.
nearest_known: Prototypical networks (Snell 2017). Difference: the prototype is formed with no role labels, by self-bootstrapped attention EMA, and it serves as the pool query of a per-line writer.
prediction: Novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.68, with person-lost errors at about 30%. Familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.95.
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: Assign the person role to the token that none of the learned role prototypes (filler, relation, value) claims, using a per-token softmax over roles in which the 'new entity' role has no prototype, only a learned constant logit.
mechanism: For each token i, compute logits l_i = [P_f s_i, P_r s_i, P_v s_i, b]. P_f has 8 rows (filler prototypes), P_r has 4 rows, P_v has 24 rows, and each group is max-reduced to one logit. b is a single learned scalar for the person role. Take a softmax over these 4 role logits per token, not over tokens. Person weight a_i = softmax_i[person] times c_i, where c_i = sigmoid(w·s_i) is a weak content gate. Normalize a over the 10 tokens. Key = A·(Σ a_i s_i) + B·(Σ r_i s_i), where r_i is the relation-role mass. Value = C·(Σ v_i s_i), using the value-role mass. Parameters: about 36·32 + 16·64 + 32·32 ≈ 3.2k. Train end to end with answer cross-entropy.
why_novel_names: An unseen name has no learned prototype, so no recognizer can claim it and it falls into the default person role by elimination. Familiar names are pushed into that role in the same way, because nothing ever learns a name template.
nearest_known: Slot attention (softmax over slots per input) and type-aware role projections. Here the competition is over fixed role prototypes plus one prototype-free default role, so the person is defined as unclaimed mass, not as a match to a learned role direction.
prediction: Novel-name person-lost errors fall from about 43% to about 20%. Novel accuracy rises to about 0.72. Familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.97.
lens: hippocampal indexing and pattern separation

core_operation: Time-cell ordinal addressing: give each token a soft rank equal to the cumulative count of content mass before it, and read roles from that rank instead of from token content.
mechanism: Content gate g_i = sigmoid(MLP(s_i)), with a small MLP of 32→32→1. Soft rank ρ_i = Σ_{j<i} g_j, computed as a cumulative sum over positions. Role tuning curves: w^k_i = g_i·exp(-(ρ_i - μ_k)^2 / 2σ^2) for k ∈ {0, 1, 2}, with learned μ_k and σ, normalized over tokens. Each pooled vector is z_k = Σ w^k_i s_i. Key = Σ_k A_k z_k with A_k of size 16×32. Value = Σ_k C_k z_k with C_k of size 32×32. A learned 3-way softmax mixes the ordinal roles into key and value. Parameters ≈ 5k.
why_novel_names: If content tokens keep a canonical order, the person's slot is fixed by how many content tokens precede it. That count needs only a generic 'is this content?' gate, which is a role-free judgement that transfers to random new tokens.
nearest_known: CoPE (contextual position encoding, Golovneva et al. 2024) uses cumulative sums of gates for positions inside attention. Here the cumulative count is used directly as a hippocampal time-cell role code that selects which token feeds the key. It is not a positional bias inside attention.
prediction: If content order is canonical, novel-name person-lost errors drop to about 10% and novel accuracy reaches about 0.85. If order is random, the gain is about 0 (fallback to the seed). The learned σ diagnoses which case holds.
lens: hippocampal indexing and pattern separation

core_operation: Content-blind relational addressing: choose the person token using only the 10×10 cosine-similarity geometry of the line, never the raw state, and pass identity to the key through a linear path.
mechanism: Compute the Gram matrix G_ij = cos(s_i, s_j) for each line. Per-token descriptor d_i = [sorted row G_i (10), G_{i,i-1}, G_{i,i+1}, ||s_i||, mean_j G_ij], 14 numbers. Selection score e_i = MLP(d_i) with sizes 14→32→3, giving three role scores. Each role score gets its own softmax over tokens, producing pooled vectors z_p, z_r, z_v. Key = A z_p + B z_r, linear with no bias or nonlinearity. Value = C z_v. Parameters ≈ 2.7k.
why_novel_names: Any random name embedding produces the same similarity profile as a familiar one: near-orthogonal to the fillers and correlated with its mixed neighbours. A selector that only sees cosines therefore cannot memorize which 16 names it was trained on. The linear key map is equivariant, so a new identity is carried through unchanged.
nearest_known: Relation networks and self-attention-then-pool also use pairwise terms, but they feed content into the pooling. Here the addressing network's input is strictly the similarity geometry, and content enters only through the linear readout.
prediction: Novel-name person-lost errors fall to about 25%. Novel accuracy rises to about 0.68, with a near-zero familiar–novel gap in pointer accuracy.
lens: hippocampal indexing and pattern separation

core_operation: Pattern-separation-invariant gating: split each state into a learned role subspace and an identity subspace, and let the selection score see the identity subspace only through its norm.
mechanism: Learn projections R (8×32) and U (24×32), regularized toward orthogonality with an orthogonality penalty added to the cross-entropy loss. Per-token features f_i = [R s_i, ||U s_i||, ||U s_{i-1}||, ||U s_{i+1}||]. Role scores = MLP(f_i) with sizes 11→32→3, then a softmax over tokens for each role. Key = K·(U z_p) + K'·(R z_r), where z_p and z_r are the pooled states. K maps 24→16 and is purely linear. Value = C z_v. Parameters ≈ 3k.
why_novel_names: Within U, name identities are random directions with similar norms. A score that depends only on ||U s|| is invariant to any rotation of identity space, so a novel name scores the same as a trained one. Meanwhile the key keeps U s equivariantly, so the dentate-like separated identity survives.
nearest_known: Capsule networks (vector length as existence) and role-specific projections. There is no routing here; the length invariance is used to make token selection blind to which identity is present.
prediction: Novel-name person-lost errors fall to about 22%. Novel accuracy rises to about 0.70.
lens: hippocampal indexing and pattern separation

core_operation: Pattern-completion source localization: score each token by how well its state, passed through a learned model of the reader's neighbour mixing, reproduces the state of its own neighbours.
mechanism: Learn a mixing model M (32×32) and a filler baseline vector m. Source score q_i = cos(M s_i, (s_{i-1} + s_{i+1})/2 - m), with zero padding at the ends. True content tokens spread their content into neighbours, so their neighbours contain M s_i. Combine with a weak role head: logits_k = α_k q_i + h_k(s_i), where h is a linear layer 32→3, with a softmax over tokens per role k. Key = A z_p + B z_r. Value = C z_v. Parameters ≈ 3k.
why_novel_names: The neighbour-mixing rule belongs to the frozen reader, not to any name. Once M learns that rule, a never-seen name still shows up as a source whose trace completes its neighbours, so it is found by its context-reinstatement signature, not its identity.
nearest_known: Seed attention pooling with a content query, and CA1-style comparator or novelty gating. Here the score is a learned inverse of the reader's mixing applied across positions: a source-versus-receiver test that needs no novelty statistic and no write gate.
prediction: Novel-name person-lost errors fall to about 18%. Novel accuracy rises to about 0.75.
lens: hippocampal indexing and pattern separation

core_operation: Pick the person, relation and value tokens by forward-backward (BCJR) decoding on a trellis whose states record which roles are already used, so the line must contain exactly one token of each role.
mechanism: Trellis states are the 8 subsets of {P,R,V} already emitted. At position i a token takes role filler, P, R or V, and a role may be taken only if its bit is unset. The path must end in state {P,R,V}. Emission log-scores come from an MLP 32->32->4 per token. Branch metrics add a low-rank coupling (u_a.x_i)(v_b.x_{i+1}) for each adjacent role pair (a,b), which models the reader's neighbour mixing. Forward-backward in log space gives posteriors q_i(role). Pool p=Σq_i(P)x_i, r=Σq_i(R)x_i, v=Σq_i(V)x_i. Key = Wk[p;r] (64->16). Value = Wv v (32->32). The whole thing is differentiable and trained by answer cross-entropy only, with about 4.5k parameters.
why_novel_names: Relation tokens (4) and value tokens (24) come from seen vocabularies and decode confidently. Fillers also decode confidently. The trellis then forces the one leftover content position to be P even when its own emission score is weak because the name is unseen. The person is found by elimination, which does not depend on the name.
nearest_known: CRF/HMM sequence taggers, and from the list, top-k/sparsemax token selection. The difference: a hard combinatorial exactly-one-per-role constraint is enforced by trellis states, and pooling uses exact marginals learned with no role labels. Independent per-role pools cannot transfer certainty from R and V onto P.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to about 15%; novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.75.
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: Exchange extrinsic role beliefs between two component decoders in a turbo loop: one reads a token's own state, the other reads only its neighbours' mixing traces, and each passes on only the information it added.
mechanism: There are two decoders. D1 reads x_i and D2 reads [x_{i-1};x_{i+1}] (zero-padded at the ends). Each is an MLP that also takes the incoming prior logits and outputs 3 role logits per position. Iterate T=3 times: L1 = D1(x_i, e2) and e1 = L1 - e2; then L2 = D2(nbrs, e1) and e2 = L2 - e1. Final role logits are L = s0 + e1 + e2, softmaxed over positions per role. Pool person, relation and value states, then key = Wk[p;r] (64->16) and value = Wv v. Parameters: D1 about 1.5k, D2 about 2.5k, Wk/Wv about 2k. Train end-to-end on answer cross-entropy. Use extrinsic dropout (randomly zero e1 or e2) so neither decoder learns to echo the other.
why_novel_names: D1 alone overfits the 16 name vectors. D2 sees a position only through how its neighbours are perturbed, and that pattern exists for any content token, including unseen names. Subtracting priors keeps D1's name-specific overconfidence from being fed back as false evidence, so D2's name-independent evidence can override it on novel names.
nearest_known: Turbo decoding (Berrou 1993) and iterative refinement in slot attention. The listed slot attention iterates one competition over the same evidence. Here two decoders see disjoint evidence (the token versus its neighbours) and exchange only extrinsic (prior-subtracted) logits.
prediction: Novel-name person-lost errors drop from 43% to about 22%; familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.97.
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: Decide token roles by soft minimum-distance decoding of a binary error-correcting role codeword computed from many weak hyperplane bit tests.
mechanism: Learn B=15 bit tests per token, b_k(x) = tanh(w_k.x + c_k). Fix a codebook C in {±1}^{4x15} for roles {filler, P, R, V}, taken from a shortened simplex code with minimum Hamming distance 8. The role score is s_i(r) = C_r.b(x_i)/B, the soft correlation decoder. Pool weights are a softmax over positions of s_i(r) for r in {P,R,V}. Then key = Wk[p;r] and value = Wv v. During training, randomly erase 3 of the 15 bits (set to 0) per token per line. Add a small penalty keeping bit tests decorrelated across tokens, so each codeword bit carries independent evidence. Parameters about 2.5k; trained only by answer cross-entropy.
why_novel_names: A bit test that latched onto a direction specific to the training names gives a wrong sign on an unseen name. With minimum distance 8, up to 3 such corrupted bits still decode to P. Erasure training forces the P decision to rest on many independent tests rather than one name-specific direction.
nearest_known: Error-correcting output codes (Dietterich and Bakiri 1995) for supervised classification. Here the code is a latent role pointer inside the pooling, learned without role labels, with bit erasure as the training channel. The listed attention pooling uses a single dot-product score per role.
