prediction: Novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.68; person-lost errors on novel names fall to about 30%.
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: Use Chase-style list decoding: enumerate a few candidate (person, relation, value) position triples by flipping the least reliable decisions, then score each with a parity-like check of the neighbour-mixing traces.
mechanism: A reliability MLP (32->24->3) gives per-position role logits. Build the hard-decision triple, then form L=12 alternatives by swapping in the 2nd or 3rd best position for the least reliable roles (Chase-II). Each hypothesis h=(p,r,v) gets a check score: for each chosen content position c and its neighbours j=c±1, compute cos(x_j - m, A x_c). Here A (32x32) is a learned estimate of the mixing map and m is a learned filler mean. Hypothesis metric = sum of chosen reliability logits + λ × sum of check scores. Weights are w_h = softmax over hypotheses. Card = Σ w_h (Wk[x_p;x_r], Wv x_v). Parameters about 4k.
why_novel_names: The check asks whether the neighbours carry a trace of whatever vector sits at the candidate position under the fixed reader mixing. That holds for any vector, seen or unseen. A novel name with a weak role score therefore regains its slot when its neighbours show the trace pattern that true content produces.
nearest_known: The Chase algorithm (1972) and, from the list, top-k/Gumbel hard token selection. Top-k selects tokens independently. Here whole joint role assignments are enumerated around a reliability ordering and re-ranked by a cross-token consistency check, then soft-combined.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names drop from 43% to about 20%.
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: Train only the role-selection pathway under jamming noise injected into the writer's own estimated name subspace, while content is read from clean states.
mechanism: Keep an EMA covariance (training-only buffer, 1k numbers) of the writer's soft person vector p across batches. Take its top-6 eigenvectors U, which approximate the subspace spanned by the 16 training names. For each line, with probability 0.6, form jammed states x̃_i = x_i + U z_i, where z_i ~ N(0, σ²I) per token and σ is matched to the name variance along U. Compute pool or role weights from x̃ (any scorer, e.g. an MLP plus softmax per role). Pool content from the clean x and build key = Wk[p;r], value = Wv v as usual. At test time use no jamming. Parameters about 3k plus the discardable buffer.
why_novel_names: An unseen name differs from training names mostly along name-identity directions. Jamming those directions during training forces the selector to locate the person from structure that survives the jam: content-versus-filler statistics, neighbour traces and exclusion of R and V. That structure is the same for novel names.
nearest_known: Feature-noise or dropout augmentation and adversarial invariance training. Here the noise is anti-jam style, confined to a self-estimated name subspace and applied only to the selection pathway. Content stays clean, so the key still carries exact identity.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from 43% to about 25%, with familiar accuracy at or above 0.96.
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: Frequency analysis (index of coincidence): weight each token by how rarely its state is repeated elsewhere in the same line, so unique content tokens are separated from repeated filler without knowing any identity.
mechanism: Compute a shared linear map z_i = A x_i (A is 32x16). Form a kernel Gram K_ij = exp(beta*cos(z_i, z_j)) for i != j, with beta learned. Set multiplicity m_i = sum_j K_ij and uniqueness u_i = sigmoid(g - h*log m_i), with g and h learned scalars. Key = sum_i softmax_i(q.x_i + log u_i) * Wk x_i. Value = sum_i softmax_i(q'.x_i + log u_i) * Wv x_i. Fillers that repeat across the line get low u_i, whatever the person token is. The person, relation and value tokens stay high. A tiny learned relation/value detector then picks the person among the survivors. Parameters: about 3k.
why_novel_names: Uniqueness is computed only from within-line coincidence. It never compares a token to a stored name, so an unseen name token is as 'unique' as a familiar one. It never falls out of the content set merely because it is unfamiliar.
nearest_known: Covariance/bilinear pooling and relation networks also use a pairwise Gram. The difference is that the Gram is collapsed to a per-token multiplicity scalar that gates the attention logit, rather than being pooled as a feature. The idea is the classical Kasiski / index-of-coincidence test.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to about 33%, and novel accuracy rises from about 0.57 to about 0.64. This holds only if filler states repeat across lines; if they do not, the gain is near zero.
lens: cryptography: keyed permutations

core_operation: Lexicographic rank canonicalisation: sort tokens in two stages by learned scalar scores, then read the person from the residual rank slot, so the role is assigned by ordinal rank and not by score magnitude.
mechanism: Stage 1: a scalar content score c_i = w1.x_i. Use a differentiable sort (NeuralSort or SoftSort, temperature annealed) to take the top 3 tokens as a 3x32 block. Stage 2: within the block, compute r_i = w2.x_i (relation-ness) and v_i = w3.x_i (value-ness). Soft-sort by r_i descending to give slot 1 = relation. Among the remaining two, soft-sort by v_i to give slot 2 = value and slot 3 = leftover (the person). Key = Wk_rel*slot1 + Wk_per*slot3, with slot 3 passed through a near-identity 32->16 map. Value = Wv*slot2. About 4k parameters, trained end to end by cross-entropy.
why_novel_names: The person is defined by elimination and rank, so an unfamiliar vector with an odd score still lands in slot 3. This holds as long as relation and value rank above it on their own detectors, and both are familiar token types.
nearest_known: SortPooling (DGCNN) and NeuralSort sort by one score and read fixed slots. The difference is the two-stage lexicographic sort with a residual elimination slot. It is not top-k hard selection, because the rank is used to assign roles.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 8 points (43% to about 35%). Familiar accuracy drops by less than 0.02.
lens: cryptography: keyed permutations

core_operation: Isometric keyed permutation: send states through a hard-constrained orthogonal (Cayley / Stiefel) channel map, so inner products with any vector, seen or unseen, are preserved on the way into the key.
mechanism: Learn a bias b (32), a skew-symmetric S (32x32), and Q = (I-S)(I+S)^-1, an exactly orthogonal matrix. Key path: t_i = Q(x_i - b), then take the first 16 channels, so the key map is a partial isometry. Pool with the usual attention weights and add a learned scalar gain per channel group (16 gains, bounded). Value path uses a separate free linear map. Even-Mansour-style whitening with b and Q means no direction in state space can be amplified or suppressed beyond a bounded gain. Training on 16 names therefore cannot build name-specific filters inside the key map. Parameters: about 1.5k for the key path.
why_novel_names: A free key matrix learns large gains on the 16 familiar name directions, and the novel-name direction then gets a diluted key contribution. An isometry keeps a novel name's cosine with the question vector equal to what the reader gave it. Person content in the key is not attenuated.
nearest_known: Orthogonal-weight regularisation (Parseval networks, orthogonal RNNs) constrains weights. The difference is a hard Cayley isometry used specifically as the key encoder, combined with an Even-Mansour pre-whitening offset. It is not a contrastive key loss or LayerNorm of keys.
prediction: The familiar-minus-novel gap narrows from 0.41 to about 0.30. Novel accuracy rises by about 0.05 and familiar accuracy falls by about 0.01.
lens: cryptography: keyed permutations

core_operation: Decrypting the reader's diffusion layer: invert the banded neighbour mixing along the position axis with an unrolled Jacobi inverse before any pooling.
mechanism: The reader mixes each state with its left and right neighbours, which is a diffusion layer like MixColumns. Model it as x = (I + L P_left + R P_right) e, where P_left and P_right are position shifts and L, R are 32x32 channel matrices. Learn L and R initialised near zero, about 2k parameters. Recover the unmixed states with 3 Jacobi sweeps: e^(t+1)_i = x_i - L e^(t)_{i-1} - R e^(t)_{i+1}, with zero padding at the line ends. Then apply the ordinary attention pool to e^(3). The same weights are used at every position and sweep, and there is no nonlinearity. The person trace smeared into the value token's state is cancelled, and the person token's own state is cleaner.
why_novel_names: The inverse is a linear operator on neighbour states, and it is the same for every token identity. It cannot memorise names. It restores the person's own state to the form the key map expects, even for unseen vectors.
nearest_known: Conv line encoders and graph deconvolution use similar structure. The difference is weight-tied inversion of a banded operator by fixed-point sweeps, initialised at the identity and used purely as pre-pooling cleanup. Nothing is added after the sweeps.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 5 points (43% to about 38%). Familiar accuracy stays at about 0.98.
lens: cryptography: keyed permutations

core_operation: Robust background cancellation with a per-channel median across the line's 10 tokens, taken as the filler baseline, so content tokens show up as residuals independent of identity.
mechanism: Compute the per-channel median over the 10 tokens, m (32 numbers). Seven of the ten tokens are filler, so m approximates the filler state. Set residual r_i = x_i - m and norm n_i = ||r_i||. Attention logits for the key pool are a_i = alpha*log(n_i + eps) + q.r_i. Key = sum softmax(a)_i Wk r_i, and the value pool uses its own q' on the same residuals. A learned relation detector suppresses the relation token in the key's person channel through a subtraction term, leaving person and value among the high-residual tokens. Parameters: about 2k.
why_novel_names: Residual magnitude against the filler median does not depend on which name token it is. A novel name deviates from the filler baseline just as a familiar one does, so it is selected as content even though nothing about it was seen in training.
nearest_known: Mean/max pooling and LayerNorm/whitening are the closest items. The difference is a median (order-statistic) baseline fitted per line and per channel. It is subtracted before attention, so it gives robust content-versus-filler separation without learned dictionaries.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 6 points (43% to about 37%). Novel accuracy is about 0.62.
lens: cryptography: keyed permutations

core_operation: An in-forward germinal-centre reaction: per line, a small population of receptor vectors is mutated, scored for affinity against the line's tokens, and resampled for a few rounds, and the matured receptor (the antibody itself) becomes the person part of the key.
mechanism: Learned germline receptor r0 (32). Per line: P=8 clones r_p = r0 + σ·ξ_p, with fixed reparameterised noise. Fitness_p = logsumexp_i(r_p·h_i)/τ − mean_i(r_p·h_i), meaning it binds one token strongly and the line weakly. Light-zone selection: clone weights π = softmax(fitness). Dark-zone step: the new mean m = Σ π_p r_p plus a pull toward the captured antigen, m += η·Σ_i softmax(m·h_i) h_i. Resample clones around m and run T=3 rounds. Key = W_k [m_T ; Σ_i a_i h_i], where a is the final binding softmax and W_k is 16×64. Value = attention read with a separate value receptor. Everything is differentiable by reparameterisation. About 3k parameters.
why_novel_names: The key is a receptor fitted to this line's antigen at test time, not a fixed detector trained on 16 names. An unseen name direction is absorbed into m through maturation, so the key carries that direction even though no weight ever saw it.
nearest_known: Slot attention with one slot (iterated attention-weighted query update). The difference is a stochastic mutate-and-select population with a contrastive fitness (one strong binder against the line mean), and the matured query itself is emitted as the key.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names drop from about 43% to about 30%. Novel accuracy goes from about 0.57 to about 0.66.
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: Absolute ligand discrimination by adaptive sorting: each token's person score is the ratio of a 'deep-state' detector energy to a 'total-occupancy' energy on the same token, so it measures quality of binding and is invariant to evidence quantity or magnitude.
mechanism: Two learned non-negative detectors per token: C1_i = softplus(u1·h_i)+ε (total occupancy) and CN_i = softplus(U_N h_i)·softplus(u1·h_i), the N-step deep state with U_N of size 4×32 summed. Adaptive-sorting output: q_i = CN_i / (C1_i + κ·Σ_j C1_j/10). This is an incoherent feed-forward loop: the activator and the inhibitor share the same input, so dose cancels. Pool weights a = softmax(β·log q). Key = W_k Σ a_i h_i (16×32). Value comes from a separate standard pool. Under 3k parameters.
why_novel_names: Novel names enter the reader at unfamiliar norms and directions, and an additive scorer misranks them by sheer magnitude. The ratio removes the overall response level, so a weak or odd-scaled unseen name is still ranked by its role 'quality' and not by how strongly the familiar detectors fire.
nearest_known: Kinetic proofreading cascade, which multiplies K gates. Here a token's own deep-state response is divided by its own occupancy plus the line occupancy, the Lalanne–François adaptive-sorting circuit. That is ratio-based dose invariance, not exponential amplification. It is also not CFAR, which normalises by the other cells.
prediction: Novel accuracy goes from about 0.57 to about 0.63, mostly through fewer person-lost errors (43% to about 35%).
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: Thymic positive-selection window: the person is chosen by a non-monotonic band-pass on a learned familiarity scalar, so it is the token of intermediate affinity, neither filler-low nor the strongly familiar relation and value.
mechanism: A learned scalar affinity f_i = v·h_i + small MLP (32→16→1). Person weight w_i ∝ exp(−(f_i − μ)²/(2s²)), with μ and s learned and renormalised over the 10 tokens. Relation and value pools use ordinary softmax on their own scorers. Training adds a margin term derived from answers alone: none, the band is learned end to end through cross-entropy. Key = W_k Σ w_i h_i. Value from the value pool. About 2k parameters.
why_novel_names: A max-selector trained on 16 names learns 'high score means one of my names', and an unseen name scores low and loses. In the band, being less familiar than relation and value but more content-like than filler is enough. An unseen name naturally lands in this window, and familiarity is not rewarded.
nearest_known: Temperature and entropy tricks on pool weights, or sparsemax. Those are monotone in the score. Here the weight peaks at a learned interior score and falls for higher scores, so it selects by an intermediate position on one axis.
prediction: Novel accuracy rises to about 0.65 while familiar stays at 0.96 or above. Person-lost errors on novel names fall to about 32%.
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: Homeostatic tonic-signal constraint: every hidden unit of the person selector must reach the same peak response in every line, so units that fire only for particular names are starved and suppressed.
mechanism: Selector hidden units z_ui = relu(A h_i), with A of size 32×32, give scores s_i = c·z_i. Per line, peak_u = max_i z_ui (soft max via logsumexp). Training loss = CE + λ·Σ_u Var_batch(peak_u)/Mean_batch(peak_u)². A homeostatic gain g_u also multiplies each unit and is updated with the running mean, as an IL-7-like set point. No name labels are used: a name-specific unit has high variance of its per-line peak because only some lines contain its name, while a role unit peaks equally in every line. Key and value come from the resulting pool. About 1.5k parameters.
why_novel_names: Every line has exactly one person, so a unit that tracks person-role structure peaks in every line, including lines with an unseen name. The regulariser removes exactly the units whose firing depends on which name is present, and those units fail on novel names.
nearest_known: Gradient-reversal identity adversary or rate-limited type code. The difference is a label-free per-unit cross-line peak-variance penalty (a lifetime-ubiquity constraint) and not an adversary or a bottleneck. It is distinct from the write gates and LayerNorm items.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names drop from 43% to about 28%, and novel accuracy reaches about 0.68.
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: AIRE-style promiscuous self-expression: during training, real person-token states from other lines are spliced into filler positions of a line, so name-like content appears in non-person roles and the selector must locate the person by context.
mechanism: Training only. For each line in a batch, with probability p=0.5, take the state at the true-content positions of another line, identified softly by that line's own top-3 content weights from the current writer (no labels). Overwrite one random filler position of the current line with that state, rescaled to the local norm. The answer target is unchanged. The writer is an ordinary selector plus key and value heads, about 4k parameters, trained by answer cross-entropy on spliced and clean lines. At test time nothing is spliced.
why_novel_names: If 'looks like a training name' no longer implies 'is the person', the selector cannot win on name identity. It must use line-internal cues: neighbour-mixing traces with the relation and value, and which token those traces bind to. These cues transfer to unseen names. The thymus does the same thing: presenting peripheral self antigens out of context forces recognition by context.
nearest_known: Thymic education (swap the selected token for a random vector) and alpha-renaming. The difference is that real familiar content states are inserted as decoys at filler positions, so name presence is decoupled from role. Neither the person token nor its rotation is replaced.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall to about 30%, novel accuracy reaches about 0.65, and familiar accuracy changes by less than 0.02.
lens: immune-system recognition of the never-seen

core_operation: A generalized-likelihood-ratio matched-subspace detector along the token axis: the reader's neighbour-leak shape is the known template, the signal direction is maximised out, and the resulting energy ratio is the person score.
mechanism: Learn a 3-tap positional leak shape g = (g-1, g0, g+1), unit norm, shared over channels. For each position t take the 3x32 patch N_t = [h_{t-1}; h_t; h_{t+1}], zero-padded at the edges. The MLE of the unknown source vector is x_t = g^T N_t (32 numbers). The GLRT statistic is T_t = ||x_t||^2 / ||N_t||_F^2, which lies in [0, 1] and measures how much of the patch fits the leak shape. Compute T_t in K=4 learned 32x8 projection subspaces, using P_k N_t in place of N_t. A tiny MLP maps the 4 statistics to logits for person, relation and value, and a softmax over t gives the weights. The key is the weight-pooled W_k x_t, so the person estimate also gathers the trace leaked into the neighbours. The value head is the seed pool. Total parameters are about 2,000.
why_novel_names: The statistic is a ratio that maximises over every possible source direction. A new name direction therefore scores exactly as high as a training name if it leaks with the reader's shape. Selection depends on the physics of the mixing, not on which 32-vector is present.
nearest_known: Quadrature-pair energy detector (a learned filter bank over feature space) and the RAKE combiner (anchored on the value token). This method filters over position with a free signal direction, uses a normalised GLRT ratio, and needs no anchor token.
prediction: Novel-name accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.68. Person-lost errors on novel names fall from 43% to about 30%.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Phase congruency along the token axis: multi-scale complex quadrature filters run over the 10 positions, and a token is salient when the filter phases align across scales, scored by the dimensionless ratio of summed local energy to summed amplitude.
mechanism: Build S=3 positional log-Gabor-style complex filters of lengths 3, 5 and 7, with learned real and imaginary taps shared over the 32 channels. Convolve the state sequence with each filter to get complex 32-vectors E_{s,t}. Phase congruency is PC_t = ||Σ_s E_{s,t}|| / (Σ_s ||E_{s,t}|| + ε), with a learned noise threshold subtracted from the numerator and then rectified. Compute PC_t in 4 learned 32x8 subspaces. Feed these 4 numbers, plus the phase angle of the summed response, to a small MLP that gives role logits. Pool the key from the raw states with the person weights and the value from the value weights. Parameters are about 1,500.
why_novel_names: Phase congruency is invariant to contrast and magnitude, and it is rotation-invariant within each subspace. A novel name that produces a weaker or differently oriented response still produces aligned phases at its position, so the selector cannot memorise the amplitudes or directions of the 16 training names.
nearest_known: Foote checkerboard novelty and quadrature energy detection. Foote uses a self-similarity matrix and quadrature detection uses energy. This method uses cross-scale phase alignment of positional filters, a ratio with no energy term.
prediction: Novel-name accuracy reaches about 0.66. The gap between familiar and novel accuracy narrows by about 10 points.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Onset-style soft non-maximum suppression: a token's weight is its contentness times the product of soft tests that it beats each neighbour within a refractory window, so selection depends on local peakedness rather than absolute score.
mechanism: A small scorer gives a contentness curve s_t over the 10 positions. Peakedness is p_t = Π_{1≤|k|≤2} σ(β(s_t − s_{t+k}) − δ_k), with learned β and margins δ_k. The adaptive onset threshold is a_t = σ(s_t − mean_{|k|≤3} s_{t+k} − λ), and the candidate mass is c_t = p_t·a_t. Role logits come from a second scorer, but they are added only as log c_t + r_{role,t}. The key and value are pooled with these weights. During training, randomly scale s by a factor in [0.3, 1] per line, so that only the relative peak shape matters. Parameters are about 3,000.
why_novel_names: A familiarity-biased scorer gives an unseen person a lower absolute score, but that token still beats its own neighbours, which carry only its weak leak. The relative local-maximum test therefore keeps the novel person as a candidate, whereas a softmax would hand its mass to the familiar value token.
nearest_known: Canny hysteresis (strong seeds plus adjacency linking) and CFAR (normalisation by background cells). This method uses multiplicative local-max suppression within a refractory window and adds no thresholded linking or clutter normalisation.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from 43% to about 32%. Familiar-name accuracy stays at or above 0.97.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: A bidirectional Kalman innovation detector: a learned linear filler-dynamics model runs along the line, each token is scored by its normalised innovation squared, and the key is built from the innovation vector, not the raw state.
mechanism: Learn a filler state model with an 8-dimensional latent: z_{t+1} = A z_t + noise and h_t = C z_t + noise, with diagonal Q and R. Run a forward and a backward Kalman filter over the 10 states; the gains are a closed-form 32x8 product per step. The innovation is e_t = h_t − C ẑ_{t|t-1}, and its predicted covariance is S_t = C P C^T + R. The NIS score is e_t^T S_t^{-1} e_t, computed for both directions. An MLP on [NIS_fwd, NIS_bwd, their difference] gives role logits. The key is the person-weighted average of the whitened innovation, S_t^{-1/2} e_t, from the two directions, passed through a linear map. Parameters are about 4,000.
why_novel_names: The predictor models only the filler background, and NIS measures surprise with respect to that model. Any unseen name is as unpredictable as a training name. The innovation also removes the part of the state that neighbour leakage made predictable, so the key carries the person's own identity.
nearest_known: Pattern-completion source localisation, which predicts the neighbours from the token, and median background subtraction. This method runs a recursive state-space predictor of the filler along the line and uses whitened innovations both to score and to build the key.
prediction: Novel-name accuracy reaches about 0.64. Person-lost errors on novel names fall to about 35%.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Group-sparse blind spike deconvolution: an unrolled group-ISTA explains the line as a learned leak kernel convolved with a few sparse source vectors plus a low-rank filler term, and selection is the surviving group support.
mechanism: Model H = K * S + F, where K is a learned 3-tap positional kernel, S is the 10x32 source matrix and F = U V_t is a filler term built from a learned rank-4 basis U. Unroll 6 group-ISTA steps. Each step takes a gradient step on ||H − K*S − F||² and then applies a group soft-threshold to every row: S_t ← S_t·relu(1 − τ/||S_t||). Fit F by least squares onto U at each step. The support mass m_t = ||S_t|| gives the candidate set. A small MLP on [m_t, ||S_t||/||h_t||] gives role logits over the support. The key and value are pooled from the deconvolved source rows S_t. Parameters are about 1,500.
why_novel_names: Sparsity selects any token that the model needs as a source, whatever its direction, so an unseen name is not rejected for being unfamiliar. Deconvolution also folds the person's leaked copies back into one clean source row, which strengthens identity in the key.
nearest_known: Wiener, Neumann and Jacobi inverse filters (non-sparse un-mixing before a separate pool) and sparsemax or top-k selection (applied to scores). This method makes selection emerge from the group-L1 support of the deconvolution itself.
prediction: Novel-name accuracy reaches about 0.65. Person-lost errors on novel names fall to about 33%.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Assign tokens to roles by Sinkhorn optimal transport with fixed role cardinalities (7 filler, 1 relation, 1 value, 1 person), where the person role has no parameters and simply receives whatever mass the other roles do not explain.
mechanism: Per token, compute logits for three learned classes (filler, relation, value) from a linear map on the 32-d state. Add a fourth 'person' column fixed at 0 with no weights. Run 5 log-domain Sinkhorn iterations on the 10x4 score matrix with row sums 1 and column sums (7,1,1,1). This gives a soft assignment P. Form pooled vectors p_role = sum_i P[i,role]*x_i for person, relation and value. Key = Linear16(concat(p_person, p_relation)). Value = Linear32(p_value) plus a small term from p_person. Train with answer-only CE. The three learned classes are shared by every line, and their tokens are dense in training. Only the person column is open-ended.
why_novel_names: Multi-head pooling needs a head whose query matches the person token, and that query is fitted to 16 name vectors. Here nothing in the person path is fitted to any name. The person is found by elimination, and the one-per-line constraint forces the leftover mass onto the unexplained token even when its own logit is uninformative.
nearest_known: Slot attention and Sinkhorn/MoE routing. The difference is that the marginals are fixed role counts and one class is parameter-free, so it is a partition by elimination, not a learned competition among slots.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to about 20%; novel accuracy goes from 0.57 to about 0.75; familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.96.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Re-reference every token to a per-line coordinate-wise median across the 10 tokens, and rescale by the line's median residual norm, before any learned layer.
mechanism: For a line X (10x32), b = coordinate-wise median over the token axis. With 7 of 10 tokens being filler, b approximates the filler/background state and also cancels the shared neighbour-mixing background. Z = X - b. Let s = median_i ||Z_i|| + eps and Zhat = Z/s. Compute gate g_i = sigmoid(a*(||Zhat_i|| - theta)) with learned scalars a and theta. Run the usual single learned attention pool for key and value, but only on Zhat, with log g_i added to the logits. Only the roughly three outlier tokens compete, and they are expressed as deviations from background and not as raw states. Parameters: the seed pool plus two scalars.
why_novel_names: A learned head scores 'is this a name' from absolute coordinates, which fails when an unseen vector lands somewhere else. The median reference and the per-line scale make the outlier test depend on how far the token is from its own line's background. That test does not depend on which name it is, and the gate stays open for any new vector.
nearest_known: LayerNorm/whitening of keys and mean/max pooling. The difference is a robust order statistic across tokens within one line, used as a background reference and scale for contrast, not a normalization across features.
prediction: Fewer wrong-person attention peaks. Person-lost errors on novel names go from 43% to about 32%, and novel accuracy to about 0.66.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Constrain the key map to a semi-orthogonal (Stiefel) projection of a convex combination of raw states, so that name geometry is preserved isometrically in directions the 16 training names never occupy.
mechanism: Pool tokens with softmax attention, so the pooled vector u is a convex combination of raw states with no pre-MLP. Key = normalize(Q u), where Q is 16x32 with orthonormal rows, parameterized by a Cayley transform or Householder reflections. Q is initialized near the identity-slice and has no free scale or bias. Add a penalty that keeps Q Q^T = I, since the Cayley/Householder parameterization gives this exactly. The value path remains an ordinary unconstrained Linear32 on the pool. Parameters: about 32*32/2 for the Cayley skew matrix, plus the attention vector.
why_novel_names: An unconstrained key matrix is trained on about 16 name directions in a 32-d space. In the other directions it receives no gradient and can shrink, rotate or mix them arbitrarily. Distinct unseen names then collapse onto similar keys, which is the 'keeps the value, loses WHO' failure. An isometry keeps pairwise angles between unseen names intact, so their keys stay separable.
nearest_known: Whitening/LayerNorm of keys and orthogonal RNN weights. The difference is a hard isometry constraint on the key weights, with the stated purpose of preserving geometry off the training-name span.
prediction: Mean pairwise cosine between novel-name keys drops measurably. Person-lost errors on novel names go from 43% to about 34%, and novel accuracy to about 0.64. Familiar accuracy may drop about 0.01.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Role-by-ordinal-count addressing: build a soft cumulative count of content-like tokens along the line and pool the token whose running count is near k, which gives 'the k-th content token' with no identity test.
mechanism: Content gate c_i = sigmoid(w.x_i + b) from a linear map with weight decay. Running soft count r_i = sum_{j<=i} c_j. For slots k=1,2,3, the weight is omega_i^k = c_i * exp(-(r_i-k)^2/(2*sigma^2)), normalized over i, with sigma learned and initialized at 0.35. The slot pools are q_k = sum_i omega_i^k x_i. Key = Linear16(concat(q_1,q_2,q_3)); value = Linear32(concat(q_1,q_2,q_3)). If the generator keeps person, relation and value in a fixed order, the slot-to-role mapping is learned softly. The role rule is purely positional and relative, so it never looks at name content. Parameters: about 70 plus the two linear layers.
why_novel_names: Softmax heads must recognize the person by content. Counting recognizes it by order, which holds for every name. The only content test is the content-versus-filler gate, which depends on the filler vocabulary, and that is dense and closed.
nearest_known: Stick-breaking attention and positional/CLS attention. The difference is that addressing is by a soft integer count of gated tokens, giving rank-k selection that is invariant to where the content tokens sit.
prediction: If content order is fixed in the generator, person-lost on novel names falls from 43% to under 10% and novel accuracy rises to about 0.88. If order is shuffled, the gain is near zero, and that outcome would itself reveal the order structure.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Resample fresh random person-token vectors every training step, with matched norm and covariance, so the writer never sees a fixed set of 16 names.
mechanism: The writer architecture is unchanged (seed pool, or any of the other cards). In the training harness, at each step draw 24 name vectors from a Gaussian fitted to the mean and covariance of the real name token vectors (or random directions on the sphere with the same norm). Use them as the person-token vectors in the frozen reader and on the question side, with 70% fresh names and 30% real names. Keep value and relation tokens as they are. Labels and loss are answer-only CE. The writer can only succeed with a rule that works on arbitrary name vectors. Held-out evaluation uses the real 16 familiar and 8 novel names.
why_novel_names: The failure comes from a writer fitted to 16 specific name vectors, with person detection and key mapping living in their span. Infinite random names remove the possibility of storing name identity and make any name-dependent shortcut unprofitable.
nearest_known: Entity anonymization (Hermann et al. 2015) and embedding-noise augmentation. The difference is continuous resampling of token vectors for the person role, with covariance matched to real names, so the writer is trained on an open vocabulary and not on permuted ids from a closed set.
prediction: Novel accuracy goes from 0.57 to about 0.78, person-lost on novel names from 43% to about 22%, and familiar accuracy falls slightly, to about 0.95.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Reed-Solomon-style algebraic decoding of the line: treat position as the code axis, get 3 content spikes' locations from a Prony/Berlekamp-Massey locator polynomial, and get de-mixed content vectors from a Vandermonde (Forney) solve.
mechanism: Give position t the node z_t = exp(2*pi*i*t/10). Compute a learned scalar contentness a_t = sigmoid(w.s_t - b) per token. Form the DFT-type power sums S_j = sum_t a_t z_t^j for j=0..5. Build the 3x3 Hankel system from them and solve (with a ridge term) for the 4 coefficients of the error-locator polynomial E. Evaluate m_t = exp(-|E(z_t)|^2/tau) at the 10 nodes. Then take the vector power sums X_j = sum_t s_t z_t^j (32 complex dims, j=0..5) and solve the 3-node Vandermonde system at the 3 estimated roots, giving 3 recovered content vectors e_1..e_3 ordered by position. These are exact inverses of the random placement and partly undo neighbour mixing. A 3-way softmax over [position rank, relation-ness, value-ness] (about 12 numbers) picks the person vector for the key and the value vector for the value. Total parameters under 3k.
why_novel_names: Locations come from an algebraic solve on one learned scalar per token, so the name direction never enters the geometry. Only the final read of e_person touches the name vector, and it does so linearly.
nearest_known: Soft forced alignment / ordinal gating / Neumann de-mixing. Those are monotone DPs, prefix counts or inverse filters. This one solves a polynomial-root (error-locator) system and a Vandermonde inverse, which is algebraic decoding of an RS code with 3 'errors'.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from about 43% to about 30%, novel accuracy about 0.57 to 0.68, familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.97.
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: Rank modulation (Kendall-tau permutation codes): the key is the soft rank order of its 16 coordinates, not their levels.
mechanism: Keep the usual attention-pooled state and linear map to 16 pre-key numbers u. Replace u by its within-key soft rank r_k = sum_l sigmoid((u_k - u_l)/T), then centre and scale it, and emit r as the key. The cosine the answerer takes on r is a Spearman correlation between question and card. Anneal T during training. The value path is unchanged. Optionally add a second 16-wide pre-key from a different projection and use the mean of the two rank vectors (Borda-style). No new parameter beyond T.
why_novel_names: An unseen name vector shifts and rescales the pooled-state coordinates unpredictably (norm, offset, gain), which warps absolute key levels. Any monotone distortion of levels leaves the rank pattern unchanged, so the card of an unseen person still lands near the question's pattern.
nearest_known: LayerNorm/whitening of keys and the empirical-copula selector input. Those standardise moments or rank across tokens at the selector input. This ranks across the 16 output coordinates, on the Kendall-tau permutation-code principle, so all level information is deliberately discarded at the card.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 6 points (43% to about 37%), with a small familiar loss of at most 0.01.
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: Successive-refinement (embedded) key code: the key is trained so every zero-padded prefix of 4, 8 and 16 coordinates is itself a usable codeword.
mechanism: The writer emits the 16-number key as usual. At training time the frozen answerer is run three times, on the key truncated to its first 4 and first 8 coordinates (rest zeroed) and on the full key. The loss is CE_16 + 0.7*CE_8 + 0.5*CE_4, all answer-only. The first 4 coordinates must separate the 4 people on their own. Each later block adds refinement with its own pooled state and a residual map from the previous blocks. Gradients through the early prefix push person identity into the few dominant, coarse directions of the pooled state. A name-specific rule would need many fine directions.
why_novel_names: Person identity at the prefix must be carried by a very low-dimensional, high-energy projection. Such a projection extends to unseen name vectors by linear continuity, while a memorised 16-name lookup cannot fit in 4 coordinates.
nearest_known: Matryoshka / nested-dropout style embeddings, which are not on the KNOWN list. The ECC framing differs in that the answerer's cosine on zero-padded prefixes is the decoder, and the blocks are built as embedded codes with residual refinement rather than dropped dimensions.
prediction: Novel-name accuracy about +0.05 (0.57 to 0.62), and person-lost errors fall from 43% to about 38%.
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: A low-density generator-matrix writer: all selector and key maps use fixed, sparse bipartite graphs with an irregular degree profile, so each output is a low-degree check on the 32 state dimensions.
mechanism: Draw once a fixed random sparsity mask for every linear layer in the writer. The selector hidden layer has 24 units and the key map has 16 outputs. Each unit sees d of the 32 input dims, with d drawn from an irregular profile (60% degree 2, 30% degree 3, 10% degree 8, as in a density-evolution-optimised LDGM). Only the weights on the edges are trained. The value map stays dense. Add a small shared-edge bias so the same dims are not all covered by high-degree units. Parameters are about 150 edges for the selector and key. The remaining budget goes to the value path.
why_novel_names: A rule that memorises the 16 training name vectors needs conjunctions over many dimensions. A degree-2 or degree-3 check cannot represent it, so the selector must use few robust coordinates (type, position-trace) that extend to unseen name directions. The redundancy across checks supplies error-correction.
nearest_known: Sparse random projections / JL (an isometry prior is KNOWN). Here the sparsity is a fixed Tanner-graph support with a designed degree distribution applied to the selector as well as the key, not a norm-preserving projection.
prediction: The familiar-versus-novel accuracy gap shrinks from 0.41 to about 0.30, with a novel-name person-lost rate near 33%.
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: Costa dirty-paper precoding of the key: the writer knows the nuisance (relation and value content) that will dominate the answerer's cosine, and pre-subtracts an alpha-scaled copy of it in key space before sending.
mechanism: Compute from the pooled states a relation estimate r and a value estimate v (two softmax pools). Map both through a 16-wide linear map G (the nuisance image in key space), so S = G[r;v]. Compute the person codeword U = W p, where p is the pooled person-bearing state. Emit key = U - alpha*S, with alpha = P/(P+N) given by a learned scalar through a sigmoid (the Costa scaling). Add a unit-power normalisation of the emitted key. The person-bearing path is trained so that U carries the 'message' and alpha*S is the known interference to be avoided. This is subtraction in key space with an MMSE-style scalar, not a deflation of token states.
why_novel_names: The relation and value channels are name-independent and heavily trained, so they are cancelled reliably. This leaves the key's cosine margin to be set by the person component, which is the only part novel names change. Unseen person directions then decide between the 2 same-relation decoys instead of being swamped.
nearest_known: Deflation pursuit / echo into the key (banned). Those subtract token-level state components during pooling. This precodes the output key against estimated interference with a Costa-optimal scalar and never touches token states.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall by about 5 points (43% to about 38%).
lens: error-correcting codes

core_operation: Reflection-symmetry (halo coincidence) detector: locate a content token only from the product of the filler-removed states on its two sides, which carry two coherent weak copies of it through the reader's neighbour mixing, and never from the token's own direction.
mechanism: Learned filler template f (32) and per-channel gain g. Residuals r_n = g*(x_n - f). For each n and lags l=1,2: s_{n,l} = relu(cos(r_{n-l}, r_{n+l})) * sqrt(|r_{n-l}||r_{n+l}|). Edges use a one-sided fallback, mu*|r_{n+-1}|. Halo score h_n = sum_l lambda_l s_{n,l}, with 3 learned scalars. Contentness c_n = sigmoid(a*h_n + b*|r_n| + d). Person weight w_n = softmax over n of [log c_n + log(1 - p_fam(n))], where p_fam comes from a small prototype bank of the 4 relation and 24 value tokens. Key = W_k * sum_n w_n (x_n + beta*(x_{n-1}+x_{n+1})/2), so the averaged halo is added to the token. Value path is unchanged. About 3k parameters.
why_novel_names: The detector uses only the agreement between the two neighbours' residuals. A novel name's vector leaks identically into both neighbours whatever its direction, so no name direction is stored in the selector.
nearest_known: Pattern-completion source localization and the Foote novelty curve. Those score a token by how well it reproduces its neighbours, or by checkerboard similarity. This card scores it by neighbour-to-neighbour coincidence (a lag-2 product, a radial-symmetry transform) and never uses the token's own state.
prediction: Person-lost errors on novel names fall from 43% to about 30%; novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.68; familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.97.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Finite-rate-of-innovation spike recovery: an annihilating-filter (MUSIC/ESPRIT-type) subspace estimate of the 3 content positions in the token-axis DFT domain, using the 32 channels as simultaneous measurements. No content detector is used.
mechanism: R_n = x_n - f (learned filler template), so the line is roughly a train of 3 spikes whose amplitudes are state vectors. Take the DFT over the token axis for k=1..6: Y_k[c] = sum_n R_n[c] e^{-2 pi i k n/10}. Divide by the mixing response H_k = 1 + 2*alpha*cos(2 pi k/10) (learned scalar alpha, regularised). For a 3-spike line, sum_{l=0..3} h_l Y_{k-l}[c] = 0 for k=4..6 and all c, which gives 96 stacked equations. Estimate h as the minimum eigenvector of the 4x4 Gram of these equations (a few inverse-power steps). The position spectrum P(n) = |sum_l h_l e^{-2 pi i l n/10}|^2 is near 0 at spike positions. Soft weights u_n = softmax(-P(n)/tau). Clean spike vectors come from a Vandermonde least-squares solve. Roles come from line order, or from a small familiar-token head applied to the three recovered clean vectors only.
why_novel_names: Positions are found algebraically from the sparsity of the line. All 32 channels share one filter, so any name vector, seen or unseen, is located equally well. Only the filler template and alpha are learned.
nearest_known: Soft forced alignment and ordinal or time-cell addressing, which need per-token content detectors. Also Neumann de-mixing. The difference is that this is Prony/FRI line-spectral estimation. Positions come from a subspace null vector shared by all channels, and amplitudes from a Vandermonde solve.
prediction: Person-lost on novel names drops to about 20% when filler is near-constant after template removal; novel accuracy about 0.72. If filler tokens are diverse, the gain shrinks to about 0.60.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Topographic prominence (0-dimensional persistence): score each token by its height above the highest saddle that connects it to a taller token on the contentness landscape of the line, so the shoulders of strong peaks score zero and a weak isolated peak survives.
mechanism: Scalar landscape c_n = sigmoid(a*|g*(x_n - f)| + b), with a filler template and channel gains. For each n find the nearest strictly higher token on the left and on the right. The saddle on a side is the minimum of c between them. If no higher token exists on a side, use the line's global minimum of c. Prominence pi_n = c_n - max(saddle_L, saddle_R). Implement it with cumulative soft-min and soft-max scans at temperature T. A halo neighbour of a strong token has pi about 0, because its saddle equals itself. Person weight w_n = softmax(beta*pi_n + log(1 - p_fam(n))), using the familiar-prototype probability p_fam. Key and value are read with w. Parameters: about 70 plus the prototype bank.
why_novel_names: A novel name's detector response can be weak and below the absolute level of a strong neighbour's halo. Prominence compares the weak peak with its own local surroundings, so it is invariant to the absolute response magnitude of unfamiliar vectors.
nearest_known: CFAR and ordered-statistic detection, and Canny hysteresis. Those threshold against a clutter estimate or link weak tokens to strong neighbours. Prominence is a parameter-free topological measure that removes a weak token's shoulder instead of linking it.
prediction: Value-token halo captures fall; person-lost on novel names drops by about 6 points (43% to about 37%); novel accuracy about 0.63.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Per-line linear-predictive inverse filtering: closed-form Levinson-Durbin predictor from the line's own token autocorrelation, with the gain-normalised prediction residual as a pulse (onset) detector.
mechanism: R_n = x_n - f. Compute the lag autocorrelations r_l = sum_n <R_n, R_{n+l}> for l=0,1,2, with ridge eps*r_0. Levinson-Durbin gives order-2 predictor a1,a2 and prediction error E. These are scalars computed fresh for each line, so no name information is stored. Residual e_n = R_n - a1*R_{n-1} - a2*R_{n-2} (zero padded). Onset score o_n = |e_n|^2 / E. A pulse also leaves a negative echo at n+1, so subtract that echo: o'_n = relu(o_n - kappa*o_{n-1}) with a learned kappa. Contentness c_n = sigmoid(a*log(o'_n + 1e-3) + b). Person weight is c_n times the unfamiliarity (1 - p_fam), softmax-normalised. Key is read from x_n with the weights, and a learned scalar mixes the neighbour contribution. About 100 parameters plus the prototype bank.
why_novel_names: The predictor is re-estimated per line, and the score is normalised by the line's own prediction gain. It depends on neither name direction nor name norm, so unseen name vectors are treated like any impulse.
nearest_known: Spectral-flux or Foote novelty and Neumann de-mixing. The difference is an adaptive all-pole predictor fitted in closed form to each line's own autocorrelation, with the pulse detected in its residual (glottal-pulse detection). There is no fixed difference kernel and no inversion of the mixing.
prediction: If filler is near-constant after template removal, novel accuracy rises by about 5 points to 0.62, with person-lost about 37%. Little gain if filler tokens are heterogeneous.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Spectral-kurtosis band ownership: weight each of the 32 channels by its across-token kurtosis (is one token dominating it?). A token's score is the share of the high-kurtosis channels that it owns.
mechanism: R = g*(x - f). For each channel c, across the 10 tokens: kappa_c = mean_n R^4 / (mean_n R^2)^2 - 3. Reliability beta_c = relu(kappa_c)/(sum_c relu(kappa_c) + eps). Channel ownership own_{n,c} = R_{n,c}^2 / sum_m R_{m,c}^2. Token score z_n = sum_c beta_c * own_{n,c}. This is a per-line, data-driven band selection, as in a kurtogram for impulsive fault detection. Contentness c_n = sigmoid(a*z_n + b*|R_n| + d). Person weight w_n = softmax(log c_n + log(1 - p_fam(n))). Key and value are read with w. Only g, f, a, b, d and the familiar-prototype bank are learned.
why_novel_names: A novel name vector spreads over its own channels. Because it is the only token occupying them, those channels have high kurtosis regardless of which channels they are. The band is chosen from the line's statistics rather than from any trained name direction.
nearest_known: Robust z-score background subtraction and the copula or per-channel soft-rank input. Those standardise each channel. This card reweights channels by 4th-order impulsiveness and scores tokens by channel ownership share, a different operation.
prediction: Selection no longer depends on name directions, so person-lost on novel names falls to about 35% and novel accuracy to about 0.64. The effect shrinks if relation and value tokens own as many channels as names do.
lens: signal processing: onset and contrast detectors

core_operation: Choose the person token using only features that stay the same under any rotation of name directions: within-line Gram entries and inner products with learned prototypes of the familiar vocabulary, never the raw name direction.
mechanism: Learn 16 prototype vectors P (16x32) by answer-only CE. They are meant to cover relation, value and filler directions. For each token t build an invariant feature f_t: its norm, its cosines to its 9 line-mates sorted in descending order, its cosines to P, and the mean and max of its row in the line Gram matrix. That is about 28 numbers. A small MLP (28-64-3) gives logits for the person, relation and value pointers. The person key part is W_p times the pointed raw state, and the relation key part is W_r times the pointed raw state, so key = W_p h_person + W_r h_rel. The value comes from W_v h_val plus 0.3 W_v' h_person. Total is about 6k numbers. The pointer cannot read name identity, because a name's direction enters f_t only through dot products with familiar prototypes and with its own line-mates.
why_novel_names: Multi-head pooling scores q·W·h_t, a linear readout of the name's own embedding direction. For an unseen name that score is effectively random, so the head drifts to the value token, which carries the person trace. An orbit-invariant scorer gives an unseen name the same feature statistics as a seen one: high self-norm and low similarity to every familiar prototype.
nearest_known: Relation networks (pairwise then sum). Here the pairwise terms are sorted cosines used only to point at a token, never summed into the card. The scorer is invariant by construction, whereas multi-head pooling has a content-linear score.
prediction: Novel-name person-lost errors drop from about 43% to about 15%. Novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.78, and familiar stays at 0.97 or above.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Constrain the person-to-key projection to a semi-orthogonal (Stiefel) map via a Cayley parametrization, so directions never seen in training are preserved rather than shrunk.
mechanism: Keep any pointer, e.g. a single softmax pool for person and one for relation. Replace the free key matrix W_k (16x32) with alpha·Q[:16], where Q = (I-A)^{-1}(I+A) and A is a learned skew-symmetric 32x32 matrix (496 numbers). alpha is a learned scalar. Then W_k W_k^T = alpha²I, so every unit input direction maps to a key of bounded, near-uniform norm and no direction can be zeroed. Add a learned 16x16 orthogonal factor on the relation path, and sum the person and relation keys with fixed weights of 0.7 and 0.3. The value path stays a free 32x32 map. Total is under 3k numbers. Training is ordinary answer-only CE, with Q recomputed each step (the matrix inverse is 32x32).
why_novel_names: A free W_k trained on 16 names is only constrained on the span of those names. Weight decay then shrinks the orthogonal complement, where unseen name directions mostly live, so novel-name keys collapse toward the relation-only key and lose to the decoys. An isometry cannot discard the complement, so a novel name keeps a distinctive key component.
nearest_known: LayerNorm/whitening of keys normalizes the output statistics after the fact. This constrains the linear map itself to be norm-preserving on all directions, including untrained ones. The pointer is unchanged.
prediction: Mean cosine between a novel-name question and its correct key rises by 0.2 or more. Novel person-lost errors fall from 43% to about 28%, and novel accuracy reaches about 0.68.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Invert the reader's neighbour mixing with a learned, differentiable 10x10 banded linear solve across positions before any selection, recovering de-mixed token contents.
mechanism: Model the states as H = M X, where M = I + a·S1 + b·S2. S1 and S2 are the ±1 and ±2 shift matrices and a, b are learned scalars, optionally one pair per state dimension (64 numbers). Compute X = (M^T M + λI)^{-1} M^T H exactly. The system is 10x10 and differentiable. Concatenate [X, H] (64 dims per token) and feed it to the downstream pointer and projections: person, relation and value pools with 64→16 key and 64→32 value maps, about 6k numbers. The person trace is removed from the value token and concentrated back at the person token. The value token's X is then a clean value.
why_novel_names: Pooling cannot undo mixing. An unseen name's weak trace on the value token pulls the person head onto the value token, which is exactly the 43% failure. Deconvolution is name-independent (it depends only on positional mixing), so it sharpens the person token's identity whether or not that name was seen.
nearest_known: Conv line encoders apply a learned forward filter. This instead solves the inverse of an explicit mixing operator as a ridge least-squares system, a tied implicit layer with 2-64 parameters, so the inverse cannot overfit name content.
prediction: The share of novel-name person-pointer mass on the value token falls by about half. Novel person-lost errors drop to about 30%, and novel accuracy reaches about 0.66.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Point at the person as the open-set reject class: a per-token softmax over learned familiar types (filler, relation, value) plus a constant, input-independent reject logit.
mechanism: A per-token classifier (32-64-3, about 2.3k numbers) outputs logits for filler, relation and value. A fourth reject logit is a learned scalar c that does not depend on the token. The person pointer is the softmax over tokens of log p_reject(t). The relation and value pointers are the softmax over tokens of their own class log-probabilities. Train with answer-only CE plus two masks. First, stop the gradient from the person pointer into the classifier's hidden layer, so the type heads learn only from the relation and value usage. Second, apply input dropout of 0.2. The key is W_p h_person + W_r h_rel, and the value is W_v h_val.
why_novel_names: Multi-head pooling needs a positive detector for 'person', and with 16 names that detector is a name lookup. Relation, value and filler vocabularies are fully familiar at test time, so detectors for them transfer. An unseen name wins the reject softmax by not matching any of them, which needs no name-specific weights.
nearest_known: OpenMax-style open-set recognition, and the banned novelty-subspace pools. Here rejection uses a classifier with a constant reject logit, not a subspace residual or reconstruction error, and the pointer never learns positive person features thanks to the stop-gradient.
prediction: Novel person-lost errors fall to about 20%, novel accuracy reaches about 0.75, and familiar accuracy is about 0.97.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Assign the three content roles to the 10 tokens by entropic optimal transport (Sinkhorn) with capacity constraints, so the person role is forced off tokens already claimed by relation and value.
mechanism: Compute role-token logits L (4x10) for person, relation, value and a filler sink using a 32-64-4 MLP (about 2.4k numbers). Run 10 Sinkhorn iterations with marginals of 1 each for person, relation and value, 7 for the filler sink, and 1 for each token. This yields a doubly-stochastic plan T. The person, relation and value pointers are the corresponding rows of T. The key is W_p(T_person·H) + W_r(T_rel·H), and the value is W_v(T_val·H). The temperature is fixed at 0.1 and is not tuned. Gradients pass through the unrolled iterations.
why_novel_names: Independent heads cannot enforce exclusivity. For an unseen name the person head has no strong target, so it spreads onto the value token (carrying the trace) or the relation token. Transport constraints let the confident, familiar relation and value assignments consume their tokens first, and the leftover non-filler token is the person by elimination.
nearest_known: Slot attention and the optimal-transport kernel embedding (Mialon et al., 2021) use softmax competition or OT for aggregation. Here OT is a hard role-capacity assignment with a filler sink, used to infer the unknown role by elimination.
prediction: Novel cases where the person pointer and the value pointer overlap by more than 0.5 drop below 5%. Novel person-lost errors fall to about 18%, and novel accuracy reaches about 0.77.
lens: inversion: list precisely what multi-head pooling cannot do for an unseen name, then design for that

core_operation: Renormalization-group decimation along the line: adjacent token pairs are merged step by step, with weights set by a closed-class filler-irrelevance score, and the less irrelevant member dominates each merge, until three 'relevant' sites remain; the person is then chosen among those three sites.
mechanism: Filler-irrelevance f_i = sigmoid(w·tanh(A h_i)), with A of size 16x32. Each of 7 decimation steps does three things. (1) Bond score b_k = f_k·f_{k+1}; a softmax over the bonds of the current chain gives a soft choice of which bond to merge. (2) The merged site state is (f_{k+1}h_k + f_k h_{k+1})/(f_k+f_{k+1}), so the less filler-like member dominates. Its irrelevance is f_k·f_{k+1}. (3) The chain is rebuilt as the expectation over the bond choice, so length drops by one each step. This leaves 3 sites (S1..S3). A 3-way role head reads only each site's irrelevance, its chain index and the 3x3 cosine matrix of the sites, and outputs person and value weights. Key = Wk·(person-weighted S) + Wr·(relation-detected S). Value = Wv·(value-weighted S). About 3k parameters. Trained by answer CE only.
why_novel_names: Decimation is driven only by filler-likeness. Filler is a closed, always-familiar class, so an unseen name survives as a relevant site whatever its direction. The last choice is among only 3 sites and uses structure, not name features.
nearest_known: Token Merging (ToMe, Bolya 2023) and funnel or hierarchical pooling. Difference: merges are restricted to adjacent sites, the bond score is a product of learned irrelevances rather than similarity, the merge is asymmetric (the relevant member survives instead of averaging), and the flow stops at a fixed point of 3 relevant sites.
prediction: Novel-name person-lost errors fall from about 43% to about 25%; novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.70; familiar accuracy stays at or above 0.96.

core_operation: Born-rule interference pooling: each token carries a complex amplitude that is the sum of an own-content path and a context-only path, and its weight is |sum|^2, so content evidence counts only when it is phase-locked to the context evidence.
mechanism: Own-content path: magnitude c_i = softplus(u·tanh(B h_i)) and phase phi_i = atan2(p1·h_i, p2·h_i). Context path: d_i and psi_i come from a small MLP whose input is the mean of the two neighbour states plus the sorted cosines of token i to the other tokens; h_i itself is excluded. Amplitude a_i = c_i e^{i phi_i} + d_i e^{i psi_i}. Weight w_i ∝ |a_i|^2 = c^2 + d^2 + 2cd·cos(phi−psi), normalised over the 10 tokens. A second interference head with its own parameters gives the value weights. Key = Wk·Σ w_i h_i and value = Wv·Σ w'_i h_i. About 4k parameters. Trained end to end by answer CE.
why_novel_names: A rule that memorises the 16 names puts its evidence into the own-content magnitude and phase. On an unseen name that phase is essentially random relative to the context path, so the cross term averages to zero and cannot pull mass to a wrong token. The name-independent context path still supplies its full d^2 term.
nearest_known: Complex-valued or quantum-inspired attention (e.g. Li et al. 2019, complex word embeddings with Born-rule probabilities). Difference: the amplitude superposes two independently computed evidence channels (self and context), so selection is coherent agreement of channels, not a single complex score.
prediction: Novel person-lost errors fall from 43% to about 32%; novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.65.
lens: physics: symmetry breaking and conserved quantities

core_operation: Bogoliubov quasi-average: a name-sensitive content scorer acts only as a vanishing symmetry-breaking field. It is annealed to zero during training, so a structurally restricted selector must inherit the chosen role assignment.
mechanism: Logits are s_i = g_i + eps(t)·m_i. The structural term g_i is a small MLP on restricted inputs: the token norm, its cosines to the other 9 tokens, and contentness and relation-detector scores from closed-class detectors. The field term m_i = v·tanh(C h_i) is an unrestricted content scorer. eps(t) decays from 1 to 0 on a cosine schedule over the first 60% of training and stays 0 afterwards; at test eps = 0. During annealing, a stop-gradient KL term (no labels, weight 0.1) pulls softmax(g) toward softmax(g + eps·m). Key and value pool with softmax(s). About 3k parameters. Answer CE only.
why_novel_names: Early on, the content field breaks the 10-fold symmetry and solves credit assignment, which a structural selector alone finds hard. After the field reaches zero, the surviving rule uses only inputs that carry no name identity, so an unseen name is handled exactly like a training name.
nearest_known: Product-of-experts debiasing with a bias-only model dropped at test (Clark et al. 2019; RUBi). Difference: here the removed expert is not trained to absorb shortcuts. It is a seeding field that is continuously annealed to zero, the Bogoliubov limit, with no separate bias-model training.
prediction: Novel accuracy rises from 0.57 to about 0.68; person-lost errors fall from 43% to about 28%; familiar accuracy drops by at most 0.02.
